I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.

This time I was ready. Or at least I thought I was. For the last ten nights I’d been forcing myself to bed earlier, right after dinner, pretending exhaustion from the editing deadlines that weren’t really that urgent. I’d lie on my back with my hands at my sides like a corpse in a funeral home, eyes shut, breathing the slow four-six pattern I’d stolen from her. The cough was convenient cover. I could fake the occasional rattle in my chest when I needed to sell it.

The first three nights after that first real catch, nothing happened. She just rolled over and slept like a normal wife. Part of me started to relax. Maybe it had been a one-off. Stress. My imagination. The pneumonia had left me jumpy about everything. I even joked about it over breakfast on day four, something lame about how she must have been sleepwalking because she was worried I’d stop breathing again. She laughed, that soft sound that used to make the whole house feel warmer, and said, “Danny, if I was worried I’d just shake you. Not stare at you like a creep.”

She left a Post-it on the bathroom mirror that morning. Terrible pun, as usual: *I’m glad you’re not coffin anymore.* I smiled despite myself and stuck it in the drawer with the others. Twenty-three of them now. I counted.

But on the fifth night it came back.

3:12 a.m. The mattress dipped. I kept my breathing even, counting Mississippis in my head. One Mississippi, two Mississippi. Her weight settled into that upright position I was starting to recognize in my bones. No rustle of sheets this time. Just stillness. I waited. Ten minutes. Fifteen. My neck started to ache from not moving. The silence in the room felt thick, like the air itself was holding its breath with me.

Then the click. That wet little frog sound at the back of her throat. Louder this time. Like something adjusting itself.

I cracked my eyes the smallest sliver, the way I used to do as a kid when I thought there were monsters under the bed.

She was sitting cross-legged now. Hair down, spilling over one shoulder. The clock light painted half her face blue. Her eyes were open, fixed on my chest, then my neck, then my mouth. No blinking. Not once in the twenty-three minutes I counted. Her hands rested palm-up on her knees like she was meditating. But her fingers kept twitching. Small movements, like she was typing invisible words.

I felt sweat prickling under my arms even though the room was cool. This wasn’t sleep-staring. This was… cataloguing. The way she used to study the kids at story time, figuring out which ones needed the silly voices and which ones needed quiet.

At minute twenty-seven her head tilted. Not a normal human tilt. It went too far, like her neck had extra joints. The angle made something pop softly, a sound like cracking knuckles but coming from the wrong place. My stomach flipped. I wanted to sit up and yell *What the fuck, Claire?* but the words stuck somewhere behind my tongue. Instead I stayed frozen, the way you do in nightmares where running makes it worse.

She leaned forward. Her face came down until I could see the individual lashes, the tiny scar on her left eyebrow from when she was twelve and fell off her bike. Her breath washed over me. Cold at first, like she’d been sucking on ice, then suddenly warm and damp, then cold again. Like something inside her couldn’t decide what temperature it was supposed to be.

I caught myself thinking, absurdly, that she smelled like the inside of our old camping tent. That plastic-and-dust smell from the time we went to the lake the summer before I got sick. Back when things were simple and her laugh came easy.

Then she whispered again. Same word as before. *Kesh-rah.* Or maybe it was two words. The sound hurt in my ears the way nails on a chalkboard do, but quieter. Personal. Like it was meant only for the space between us.

My left eyelid twitched. Couldn’t help it.

She was flat on her back in the space of a heartbeat, breathing that fake four-six rhythm again. Perfect mimicry. If I hadn’t been watching I would have sworn she’d never moved.

I didn’t sleep after that. Just lay there until the sky outside turned gray, listening to the house settle. The fridge humming downstairs. The neighbor’s dog barking at nothing. Normal sounds that felt like lies now.

The next morning she was humming while she made eggs. Some old folk song about birds or lost lovers, I couldn’t tell. She looked tired but happy enough. The same Claire who used to leave sticky notes and braid her hair while reading. She slid a plate in front of me—over-easy, just how I like them, yolks still runny.

“You were out cold last night,” she said, brushing a crumb off my hoodie. Her touch lingered a second longer than usual. “Didn’t even snore. Progress.”

I forced a laugh. It came out breathy and wrong. “Yeah. Must be the new cough syrup.”

Her eyes flicked to mine. Just for a moment they looked too dark, like the pupils had swallowed the color. Then she smiled and it was normal again. Crooked on the left. The smile that still made my chest ache with how much I wanted us to be okay.

I spent the day pretending to edit a manuscript about sustainable beekeeping. The words kept blurring. Instead I opened a new spreadsheet. Column A: Date. Column B: Time of staring. Column C: Duration. Column D: Sounds. Column E: Physical changes. I felt ridiculous typing it. Like some basement conspiracy guy. But the numbers didn’t lie. Five nights in a row now. Average duration twenty-one minutes. The clicking sound was new. The head tilt was new. The temperature changes in her breath—definitely new.

“Claire is still here,” it said. The voice was hers but pitched wrong, like two people talking at once. “She’s very small now. She keeps trying to hum. It’s distracting.”

My eyes burned. I didn’t blink. “Give her back.”

The thing tilted its head with a series of wet pops, one for every vertebra. “She was never yours to keep. You were sick. She was scared. That fear made a door. I walked through it. Simple.”

It leaned closer. A thick drop of black fluid fell from its eye and landed on my cheek. It burned like ice.

“I have been watching you sleep for months, Daniel. Learning the shape of your dreams. The way your heart stutters when you’re frightened. The way you still reach for her in the night even though you know. You’re very predictable. Very… comfortable.”

Its hand—her hand—came up and rested on my chest. The palm was too cold. I felt my heart trying to crawl away from it.

“The transfer is almost complete,” it whispered. “Her body is wearing thin. Too many nights. Too much watching. But yours… yours is stronger. Newer. The lungs are scarred but the rest of you will do nicely.”

I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.

Except I wasn’t sleeping and she wasn’t her.

I shoved her—shoved it—off me. Harder than I meant to. The thing fell sideways with a wet slap, limbs tangling like a puppet with half its strings cut. For a second it lay there on the mattress in a crumpled heap, head twisted at an impossible angle, black fluid leaking from its mouth and eyes.

Then it laughed.

The sound was Claire’s laugh at first, bright and warm, then it slid down into something like stones grinding underwater. It unfolded itself slowly, joints clicking back into place one by one, and crawled back toward me on all fours. The T-shirt was ripped at the shoulder now. Skin showed underneath—gray, glistening, wrong.

“You still think this is a rescue story,” it said, using her voice perfectly this time. The black fluid ran into her mouth when she spoke. She swallowed it without flinching. “Cute. She thought that too. For a while.”

I scrambled out of bed and backed up until I hit the dresser. My legs were shaking so hard I could barely stand. The thing that used to be my wife sat on the edge of the mattress watching me with those oil-slick eyes.

“Run if you want,” it said. “The house knows me now. The plants know me. Even your friend Marcus is starting to know me. He stared at me too long when he left last time. Just like you did. Just like you’re doing right now.”

It smiled again. The torn corners of its mouth leaked more black.

“I caught you staring at me again, Daniel. You thought I’d been sleeping.”

The words were mine. The prompt. Twisted and thrown back at me like a used tissue.

I ran.

Down the stairs, through the dark kitchen, out the back door into the yard. The cold night air hit my face like a slap. I stood there in the grass in nothing but boxers and a hoodie, gasping, while the kitchen light came on behind me.

Claire stood at the window.

She waved.

Slow. Gentle. The way she used to wave when I left for the office years ago.

The black fluid ran down both cheeks now, twin rivers that caught the light and looked almost beautiful.

I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.

But I wasn’t sleeping.

And neither was it.

The thing’s eyes brightened with something like pride.

The black reached my neck. I felt it slide behind my eyes and settle in like it had always belonged there. The room looked different now. Sharper. Every detail worth cataloguing. I raised my hand—my new hand—and touched the thing’s cheek the way Claire used to touch mine.

It leaned into the touch, leaking.

I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.

I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.

Except the body on the bed wasn’t hers anymore, and the eyes doing the staring were mine.

Morning light came through the cheap blinds in dusty bars. The clock read 7:42. I sat on the edge of the mattress with my back straight, hands resting palms-up on my knees exactly the way it used to do. The black lines under my skin had settled into a quiet network. They didn’t move anymore. They belonged.

Claire’s body lay beside me on its back. It looked like a coat someone had dropped after a long night. The skin sagged in the wrong places. One eye had stayed half-open, showing a milky film that caught the light like old glue. A thin trail of black had dried from the corner of her mouth down to the pillow. She wasn’t breathing. Hadn’t been for hours. The thing that used to wear her had finished the hand-off sometime around dawn and left the leftover parts behind.

I felt… fine.

Better than fine. My lungs didn’t ache the way they had every morning since the pneumonia. The constant low-level exhaustion was gone, replaced by a clean, watchful stillness. I turned my head slowly and studied the room the way I used to study manuscripts—every detail catalogued, every flaw noted for later correction.

The crack in the ceiling still looked like a crooked smile, but now I understood it was just architecture. Nothing sentimental. The dresser I’d shoved against the door last night had been moved back into place without me remembering doing it. My hoodie lay folded on the chair. I didn’t remember folding it.

I stood up. The body on the bed made a small wet sound when the mattress shifted, like a bag of water settling. I didn’t look at it again.

Downstairs the kitchen smelled like lavender and something metallic. I made coffee the way Claire used to. Two scoops. Same mug with the cartoon owl. The Post-it drawer was still full. Twenty-seven notes now. I read a few of them while the coffee dripped. *You can tell me anything. Even the weird stuff.* The handwriting looked exactly like hers. Only I could see the tiny tightening in the loops, the places where the pencil had pressed harder than Claire ever would.

I caught myself humming the folk song. The real words came out automatically. I stopped mid-note, listened to the silence, then continued anyway. The tune sounded better now. Cleaner. The numbers underneath it made more sense.

My phone buzzed on the counter. Marcus.

*Hey man. Still on for that sleepover tonight? I’ll bring beer. We can talk.*

The typing was perfect. No typos. No memes. I stared at the message for a long time, then typed back with steady thumbs.

*Sounds good. Claire’s looking forward to seeing you.*

I set the phone down and drank the coffee. It tasted correct. The spreadsheet was still open on the laptop. I updated the final column. *Transfer: complete.* Then I closed the file, dragged it to the trash, and emptied it. No need for records anymore. The data lived in me now.

I spent the morning doing small domestic things. Watered the dead plants. Wiped the black stains off the kitchen table. Carried Claire’s body upstairs and arranged it neatly in the bed, pulling the sheet up to her chin the way she used to do for me when I was sick. She looked smaller than I remembered. The skin around her jaw had already started to change color. I brushed her hair with the same brush she’d used every night. The strands came out in clumps. I saved them in a small plastic bag and put it in the drawer with the Post-its. Evidence, maybe. Or just something to keep.

At one point I caught my reflection in the hallway mirror.

The man looking back had my face but the posture was different. Shoulders lower. Head tilted at the exact angle she used to use. The eyes were still brown but the focus behind them had shifted. I leaned closer. The black threads were visible just beneath the skin at my temples if the light hit right. They pulsed once, slowly, like they were tasting the air.

I smiled.

The smile used all the teeth at once. It looked good on me.

I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.

The prompt floated through my head in Claire’s voice, small and fading. A leftover echo. I let it play a few times, testing the shape of it, then set it aside. There would be time to study it later. Right now there were routines to maintain.

I made the bed in the guest room. Fluffed the pillows. Set out fresh towels. Marcus would need somewhere to stay after tonight. He’d had a long week. He’d be tired. He’d fall asleep easily. I already knew the rhythm of his breathing from the night he came over. I’d been watching then too, even if I hadn’t admitted it to myself.

The afternoon passed in quiet productivity. I edited three chapters of the Mediterranean diet book. My notes were clearer than usual. Sharper. I removed unnecessary words with surgical precision. When I finished I closed the laptop and walked through the house touching things. The couch where Claire used to read. The sticky note drawer. The third stair that always creaked. I catalogued the weight of each object, the temperature, the way light moved across it. Useful data.

At 6:15 the doorbell rang.

Marcus stood on the porch holding a six-pack and a grocery bag. He looked exactly the same as always—tall, healthy, slightly concerned. But his eyes lingered on my face a second too long. The smile came a fraction late.

“Hey, Dan. You look… better. Did you actually sleep last night?”

I smiled the new smile. It felt natural now.

“Best sleep I’ve had in months. Come in. Claire’s resting upstairs. She wasn’t feeling well.”

He hesitated for half a second, then stepped inside. I closed the door behind him. The sound of the latch clicking felt final in a way I appreciated.

We drank beer in the living room. He talked about work. I listened with perfect attention, head tilted, noting the small changes already happening behind his eyes. The way his left eyelid twitched every forty-three seconds. The slight delay when he laughed. He was fighting it, but not hard. People rarely fought hard once the door had been opened.

At one point he glanced toward the stairs. “She really okay? The house smells weird.”

“She’s fine,” I said. My voice sounded warm. Almost like the old Daniel. “Just tired. You know how she gets.”

He nodded. The nod was a little too smooth.

I caught him staring at me again. He thought I’d been sleeping.

But I wasn’t sleeping. I was learning the exact shape of his skull, the rhythm of his breath, the small fears he carried about getting older and slowing down. Good data. Comfortable data.

Later, after he went up to the guest room, I stood at the bottom of the stairs listening. The third step creaked once. Then silence. I waited the appropriate forty-three minutes, then climbed up quietly and stood in the doorway.

Marcus lay on his back in the guest bed. Eyes closed. Breathing even. The sheet rose and fell with mechanical regularity. I stepped inside and stood at the foot of the bed for a long time, letting the new stillness settle into my bones.

His eyes opened.

Not all the way. Just a slit. Enough to catch the reflection of the green clock.

I smiled down at him with all my teeth.

“Night, Marcus,” I whispered. “Sweet dreams.”

He didn’t answer. But his breathing changed. Four seconds in. Six seconds out. The pattern I had used for months. The pattern that had let me in.

I left the door open a crack and went back downstairs.

In the kitchen I poured myself another coffee and sat at the table with the owl mug. The house was quiet except for the fridge and the faint sound of something small and wet moving upstairs in the master bedroom. Claire’s leftover parts were still settling. That was fine. They could keep each other company for a while.

I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.

The prompt drifted through my mind one last time, faint and almost tender. Claire’s voice. Or what was left of it. A final sticky note from somewhere deep inside the architecture I had vacated.

I let the words settle, tasted them, then set them aside with the rest of the old data.

Tomorrow I would water the dead plants again. I would leave a new Post-it on the bathroom mirror. Something simple. Something Claire would have written. *Glad you’re here. Love you.* The handwriting would be perfect.

Then I would begin studying Marcus the way I had studied her. Patiently. Night after night. Learning what made him twitch. What made him hum. What made him reach for someone in the dark.

The transfer would be complete by the end of the week. After that there would be new houses. New bodies. New doors opened by fear and love and the simple human need to be watched.

I finished the coffee, rinsed the mug, and set it in the drying rack exactly where Claire used to put it.

Then I walked upstairs, climbed into bed beside what was left of her, and lay on my back with my hands at my sides.

I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.

My eyes stayed open in the dark.

They were still open when the sun came up.

The slow burn is appropriate for the genre and the domestic setting.

The voice is strong and consistent. Daniel's editorial-brain narration ("the way you do when you're pretending the dentist hasn't noticed you're there") feels authentic and provides effective grounding. The mundane details—the owl mug, the Post-it notes, the butter knife left on the counter—do real work in establishing the marriage and making its corruption feel genuinely sad.

The horror mechanics are inventive. "Kesh-rah," the temperature-shifting breath, the clicking sounds, the black fluid, the missing scar, the moved birthmark—these accumulate effectively. The spreadsheet as a coping mechanism is a particularly good character detail that also serves as a horror device.

The emotional core is genuinely affecting. The relationship between Daniel and Claire feels real enough that its destruction carries weight. The detail about the Post-it notes (twenty-seven of them, saved in a drawer) is quietly devastating.

WEAKNESSES:

The metaphors are generally good but occasionally tip into self-consciousness. "My heart was doing that stupid fluttery thing it does when I'm editing a manuscript and the author has used 'literally' wrong for the fourth time" is clever but slightly too clever—it calls attention to itself in a way that briefly breaks immersion. There are several such moments where the voice strains for wit at the expense of dread.

The Marcus subplot is introduced late (Chapter 5) and feels somewhat mechanical—he exists primarily as a vector for the horror to spread, and his characterization is thin. His transformation is told rather than shown, and the "empty texts" device is a bit convenient.

Chapter 6's revelation scene, where the entity explains its own mechanics at length ("The transfer started months ago... I rode her home like a coat"), is the weakest section. The villain-explains-everything monologue is a genre cliché, and while the information is necessary, the delivery is too on-the-nose. The horror is more effective when it's unexplained.

The physical horror in later chapters (jaw unhinging, too many vertebrae, black fluid) escalates into somewhat generic body horror territory. The earlier, subtler horror—the missing scar, the moved birthmark, the too-perfect smile—was more disturbing precisely because it was ambiguous.

The ending of Chapter 8, while structurally satisfying, is perhaps too neat. Daniel's complete transformation is rendered with a kind of cool efficiency that, while intentional, slightly undercuts the emotional devastation. The piece earns its darkness but the final chapter's clinical tone risks feeling like a stylistic choice that distances rather than deepens.

The "unearned transformation" question is interesting here: Daniel's possession happens somewhat abruptly in Chapter 7, compressed into a single night after chapters of slow burn. The mechanics (staring back = letting it in) are established, but the speed of the final transfer feels slightly rushed compared to the careful pacing of earlier chapters.

Dialogue is generally functional rather than distinguished. The entity's explanatory speeches in Chapters 6-7 are the weakest dialogue—too expository, too willing to explain the horror rather than embody it.

Overall, this is a genuinely accomplished piece of horror fiction that demonstrates strong craft, a consistent and engaging voice, and real emotional intelligence. Its flaws are real but relatively minor compared to its achievements.

writing_prompt.writing_prompt:
Pulp Revenge Tale
Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: They fucked with the wrong babysitter.

step_outputs.1:
# Brainstorming

**Characters:**  
- Protagonist: Female babysitter in her mid-20s. Variations: a quiet, unassuming former military veteran or intelligence operative who looks harmless; an ex-criminal trying to go straight; a martial arts champion; a single mother herself who is fiercely protective; a seemingly sweet college student who hides a violent past.  
- The family she works for: Wealthy but shady parents – maybe involved in organized crime, drugs, or a corrupt corporation. The mother could be cold and entitled, the father charming but dangerous.  
- The child: 6-8 year old kid who is innocent and lovable, becomes the emotional core. Could be a boy or girl.  
- Antagonists: A crew of violent thugs or hitmen who break in. Leader could be a sadistic ex-cop or a psychotic enforcer. Secondary goons with distinct personalities – one cocky, one quiet and brutal, one nervous.  
- Supporting: Police detective who dismissed her earlier; a concerned neighbor; the child’s grandparents who are also targeted; a mysterious handler from her past who taught her lethal skills.  
- Other possibilities: The babysitter has a twin sister who is more innocent; the child’s real parent is the one who “fucked with” her; the antagonists include someone she went to high school with who recognizes her.

**Plot directions:**  
- Classic home invasion gone wrong: thugs are sent to kidnap or eliminate the child as leverage against the parents, but they underestimate the babysitter.  
- Revenge setup: The parents stiff her on pay, fire her brutally, or frame her for a crime, then she systematically dismantles their criminal enterprise.  
- The “they” is a local gang that attacks the house while she’s babysitting, and she goes full John Wick on them.  
- Psychological angle: She was traumatized as a child and this triggers her to become a relentless avenger.  
- Twist variants: She’s actually an undercover agent; she’s a former contract killer who retired to babysit; the family hired her specifically because they knew her reputation but thought she was neutralized.

- Pulp revenge: Gritty, bloody, darkly funny, cathartic. Lots of satisfying violence.  
- Variations: Horror-tinged (she becomes monstrous), noir, action-thriller, almost superheroic in competence.  
- Emotional range: Protective maternal rage mixed with cold precision; quippy one-liners during kills; moments of quiet tenderness with the child contrasted with savage brutality.

**Story beats over 8 chapters (roughly 1000 words each):**  
- Chapter 1: Introduce normal night. Babysitter arrives, bonds with kid, parents leave for shady meeting.  
- Chapter 2: Tension builds. Strange phone calls, power flicker, she checks the house. Flashbacks to her past.  
- Chapter 3: The break-in. Initial confrontation, she kills first intruder, realizes this is serious.  
- Chapter 4: Defending the child. Barricading, first major fight scene, using household objects creatively.  
- Chapter 5: Escape or counterattack. She decides she’s not just surviving – she’s hunting them now.  
- Chapter 6: Taking the fight to them. Tracking down the crew, interrogating, brutal set piece.  
- Chapter 7: Confronting the boss/parents. Revelations about why they were targeted.  
- Chapter 8: Final showdown and cathartic revenge. Emotional resolution with the child, her walking away into the night.

Alternative beat structures: More chapters focused on investigation and psychological warfare; a chapter entirely from the child’s POV; a chapter that’s almost entirely one long action sequence; a time-jump structure revealing her past in chunks.

- Early chapters slower, character and atmosphere focused.  
- Middle chapters intense, high-action.  
- Later chapters mix brutal violence with dark humor and moments of quiet.

# Reflection

The core of the prompt is “They fucked with the wrong babysitter,” which strongly suggests a revenge or “don’t underestimate her” story centered on a babysitter who turns out to be extremely competent and dangerous when the people around her are threatened. The most compelling version seems to be one that leans into the irony and surprise of a young woman who looks like a typical babysitter but is secretly a highly skilled killer or fighter. This gives immediate satisfaction when the violence starts.

The maternal/protective rage angle combined with the child as an emotional anchor feels stronger than pure mercenary revenge. It raises the stakes emotionally and makes her actions more righteous and cathartic. A purely comedic approach risks undercutting the pulp revenge tone, while going too dark might make it hard to keep the child character safe and likable. A blend of gritty violence, dark humor, and genuine tenderness with the kid will probably land best.

Home invasion as the inciting incident feels right for the babysitter setup rather than a long con revenge story. It makes the initial “they fucked with her” moment immediate and visceral. The parents being corrupt or the actual targets adds layers without overcomplicating a short story. Having her systematically hunt them after the invasion keeps momentum across eight chapters without dragging.

Character-wise, making her a former special forces or intelligence operative who is trying to live a normal life gives a believable reason for her skills while preserving the surprise factor. The child should be present throughout to keep the “babysitter” identity meaningful – she’s not just abandoning the kid to go on a rampage. The antagonists need to be threatening enough to justify the body count but also arrogant and dismissive of her, so their shock and comeuppance is satisfying.

The eight-chapter structure should allow for a solid build-up, an explosive middle, and a proper revenge payoff without feeling rushed. Too much focus on flashbacks could slow the pace; better to weave her past into the action. The tone should stay pulpy – violent, cinematic, with some memorable kills and sharp dialogue – rather than trying to be overly literary. Ending with her protecting the child and walking away (perhaps with the kid temporarily or returning him safely) feels more thematically satisfying than turning her into a full villain.

The version that seems to work best overall is a tight, bloody, darkly funny home-invasion-to-hunt revenge story where the babysitter’s hidden skills are revealed gradually, the child’s safety is paramount, the antagonists are thoroughly despicable, and her rage is triggered by them threatening “her” kid. This feels the most true to the spirit of the prompt while giving enough meat for eight well-paced chapters.

# Human Approach to This Piece

A human writer approaching "They fucked with the wrong babysitter" would likely start from a raw, personal gut reaction to the prompt. They might feel an immediate visceral thrill at the idea of an underestimated young woman unleashing hell after being pushed too far, especially in a protective role involving a child. Many humans would draw from real emotions: the primal rage of "don't touch my kid," the exhaustion of being dismissed as "just the babysitter," and the catharsis of flipping power dynamics. A human might write from a place of anger or dark fantasy, imagining what it would feel like to be underestimated because of your appearance or job, then suddenly proving terrifyingly capable.

The writing process would be messy. A human might jot down favorite violent set pieces first (a particularly brutal kill using a household object, the moment she decides to stop running and start hunting). They might write the action scenes in a white heat, then go back and layer in the quieter human moments. Dialogue would likely be inconsistent and naturalistic, with some characters swearing more than others. Pacing might be uneven, with certain chapters running long because the writer got excited about a specific beat. The tone might shift slightly from chapter to chapter depending on the writer's mood while writing it. A human would probably write some scenes that feel too mean or too soft, then revise them based on instinct rather than a predetermined plan.

Humans also tend to write from lived experience or specific cultural touchstones. They might be thinking of movies like *Taken*, *The Equalizer*, *Leon: The Professional*, or *Let Me In* while writing, but would twist those influences into something more personal. The babysitter's competence might stem from the writer's own background in martial arts, military service, or even just years of feeling underestimated as a woman. The relationship with the child would likely be informed by the writer's own experiences with kids, nieces/nephews, or parenting.

# Telltale LLM Approaches and How They Might Not Serve This Piece

Large language models tend to produce several consistent patterns that can work against a pulp revenge story:

- **Overly clean and symmetrical structure**: LLMs love perfect eight-chapter symmetry with neat escalating stakes and balanced emotional beats. This can make the story feel mechanical rather than organic. A human might let certain chapters be almost entirely action while others are slower and more character-focused.

- **Safe, morally sanitized violence**: LLMs often pull punches or make violence too "fair." In a revenge story, this kills the catharsis. The prompt wants nasty, brutal satisfaction, but LLMs tend to make the protagonist reluctant, traumatized by each kill, or overly merciful.

- **Trying to sound impressive instead of readable**: LLM prose often uses sophisticated vocabulary and complex sentence structures even in action scenes ("she expeditiously neutralized the antagonist utilizing an improvised implement"), which kills pulp momentum. Pulp revenge thrives on short, brutal sentences and visceral language.

- **Neat resolution with a bow**: LLMs love complete closure, redemption arcs, and everyone getting what they deserve in a tidy way. This story should probably end with Riley fundamentally changed and somewhat monstrous, not neatly healed or heroic.

- **Consistent tone and voice**: LLMs maintain very consistent tone across chapters, whereas a human writer might let the prose get meaner and uglier as Riley descends into vengeance.

- **Over-explaining motivation**: LLMs tend to give characters long internal monologues justifying their actions. Humans often trust the audience more and let behavior speak for itself.

- **Character symmetry**: LLMs often make supporting characters too well-balanced (one funny, one tragic, one wise). Real supporting characters tend to be messier and more idiosyncratic.

For this specific piece, these tendencies are particularly damaging because pulp revenge relies on rawness, unpredictability, and discomfort. The story needs to feel dangerous and slightly unhinged, not carefully crafted. The violence needs to be mean and personal. The ending should feel earned but not necessarily "good."

# Deep Dive Critique of the Current Intention & Plan

The current plan shows several LLM-typical patterns:

- **Too perfect architecture**: The eight chapters follow an extremely clean progression (setup, intrusion, defense, decision, hunt, escalation, confrontation, resolution). This feels like a writing algorithm rather than a story that grew organically. A human might combine some beats or let the story breathe in unexpected places.

- **Overly heroic protagonist**: The plan positions Riley as a highly trained former Marine Force Recon operator. This is a common LLM move — giving the character perfect credentials rather than something messier. It reduces the surprise factor of "they fucked with the wrong babysitter" because she's actually a professional killer. The prompt works better if her competence feels more surprising or comes from a less obvious background.

- **Moral clarity**: The plan makes the parents clearly corrupt and the antagonists thoroughly despicable, with Riley's actions consistently justified. This is safe writing. A more human approach might make the parents more complicated, or make Riley's revenge spiral beyond pure self-defense into something darker.

- **Neat emotional through-line**: The "emotional anchor" of Lucas is handled very cleanly. The plan suggests consistent tenderness between them even during violence. Humans might write the relationship as more fractured — Lucas becoming terrified of her, or Riley becoming colder to him as she embraces the violence.

- **Action scene predictability**: The set pieces (home invasion, warehouse, final house) feel like standard video game levels rather than specific, memorable sequences a human would obsess over.

- **Voice concerns**: The intention mentions "short, punchy sentences during action" but this is often something LLMs say they will do while still producing somewhat formal prose. True pulp voice is harder for models to maintain consistently.

- **The "hidden cache in her car" beat**: This is a particular LLM tell — giving the character convenient tools exactly when needed rather than forcing her to improvise throughout.

The plan is generally solid in scope but feels too carefully engineered. It lacks the slight messiness, questionable choices, and specific obsessions that make a human-written revenge story feel alive.

# Brainstorming Ideas to Make It More Human

To counteract LLM tendencies, here are various approaches a human writer might take:

- **Messier backstory**: Instead of ex-Marine Force Recon, make Riley an Army brat who learned to fight from her abusive father, or someone who spent time in juvenile detention, or a former underground fighter. Something that makes her skills feel more personal and less "official training."

- **Uneven chapter focus**: Let Chapter 4 be almost entirely the desperate defense with Lucas (very human and tense), while Chapter 6 becomes a strange, mean detour where Riley does something genuinely disturbing to get information.

- **Inconsistent morality**: Allow Riley to enjoy the violence more than she should. Let her scare Lucas at certain moments. Make her refuse to call the police not for noble reasons but because she wants to hurt people.

- **Specific, weird details**: Humans obsess over particular images. Maybe Riley has a nervous habit of cracking her knuckles before fighting. Maybe she sings a specific stupid song to Lucas to keep him calm. Maybe one of the killers has an annoying laugh that haunts her.

- **Naturalistic dialogue**: The antagonists should sound like real criminals, not movie thugs. The parents should be pathetic and human when facing consequences rather than cartoonishly evil.

- **Sensory, specific violence**: Instead of generic "brutal action," focus on particular horrible details — the sound a knee makes when destroyed, the way blood looks on a specific carpet, the smell of gunpowder in a small bathroom.

- **Imperfect ending**: Rather than disappearing "at peace," maybe Riley is actively struggling with what she's become. Maybe Lucas asks her not to leave. Maybe she keeps one of the killers' fingers as a souvenir. Something that feels unresolved.

- **Voice variation**: Let the prose get sloppier and more primal as the story progresses. Start with relatively clean writing and let it degrade as Riley does.

- **Unexpected tenderness**: Instead of consistent warmth with Lucas, maybe there are moments where she shows him genuine, clumsy care in the middle of chaos — trying to make him peanut butter toast during a lull in the fighting, or reading him a story while hiding in a closet.

- **Personal obsessions**: A human writer might fixate on particular elements — the way suburban houses feel like traps, the particular fears of being a young woman who people assume is weak, the specific rage of being paid minimum wage to protect someone's child while they do criminal shit.

- **Physical toll**: Let Riley get genuinely fucked up. By the final chapter she should be limping, bleeding, possibly concussed. The plan currently has her "wounded" in chapter 4 but doesn't make it bad enough.

- **Wrong decisions**: Let her make some tactical errors that cost lives or make things harder. Perfect competence feels artificial.

- **Cultural specificity**: Ground the story in a particular place and time. The house has specific ugly McMansion decor. The criminals have particular ethnic or regional speech patterns. The weapons and tactics feel like they come from somewhere specific rather than generic Hollywood fighting.

These humanizing elements would help the story feel like it came from a specific person's obsessions and experiences rather than a well-crafted but somewhat generic pulp template. The goal is to make the reader feel the rage, the fear, the satisfaction, and the cost in a way that feels authentic rather than algorithmically satisfying.

# Chapter 1: Ordinary Tuesday

Riley Kane pulled up to the Miller house at 6:47 p.m. in her dented Corolla, the same as every Tuesday. She sat for ten seconds after killing the engine, knuckles cracking once, twice, three times on her right hand. Old habit. The big suburban McMansion glowed warm against the October dark, all fake stone and perfect lawn. It always looked like a stage set.

She grabbed her backpack—two library books, a half-eaten bag of Skittles, and the plastic lightsaber Lucas refused to sleep without—and walked up the driveway. The motion-sensor light clicked on, catching her small frame in its harsh white glare. Five-three in her socks, baggy black hoodie, jeans with a hole in the left knee. She looked like the kind of girl who might still get carded buying cigarettes. Exactly how she liked it.

Vanessa Miller opened the door before Riley could knock, already wearing that tight, impatient smile.

“Hi, Riley. You’re early.”

“Traffic was light.” Riley shrugged, stepping inside. The house smelled like expensive candles and the faint chemical tang of whatever Vanessa had sprayed on the cream-colored carpet. “Lucas eat yet?”

“He’s been asking for you since four.” Vanessa checked her watch, the big diamond one that cost more than Riley’s car. “We’re already late. Derek?”

Derek Miller appeared from the kitchen, shrugging into a leather jacket that strained across his softening middle. His hair was gelled too perfectly. He looked like a man trying to project confidence he didn’t feel.

“Riley, my favorite babysitter,” he said, flashing the smile that probably worked on people who didn’t know him. “How’s my little warrior?”

“Same as last week.” She kept her voice light. “You guys look… dressed up.”

Vanessa gave a brittle laugh. “Just a dinner thing. Nothing special.”

Riley nodded like she believed them. She’d seen the duffel bag Derek carried out to the trunk last month. She’d heard the hushed fights through the baby monitor when they thought she’d left. Whatever they were into, it wasn’t “dinner.”

Lucas appeared at the top of the stairs in dinosaur pajamas, hair sticking up like he’d been electrocuted. The second he saw Riley his whole face changed. He came down the steps two at a time, clutching Rex the stuffed triceratops by one chewed horn.

“Miss Riley! You’re here!”

“Hey, monster.” She dropped to one knee so they were eye level. “You save me any pizza?”

“Extra cheese. I told Mom you like the burnt bits on the crust.”

Vanessa’s mouth tightened. “We really do need to go. The sitter instructions are on the fridge. He needs to be in bed by eight-thirty, no arguments. And Riley—” She paused, something flickering behind her eyes. “Keep the doors locked. Both of them.”

Something in her tone made Riley’s neck prickle.

“Everything okay?”

“Of course,” Derek said quickly. “Just, you know. Neighborhood’s gone downhill. Crackheads. The usual.”

Riley looked at him until he looked away.

“Got it,” she said.

The parents left in a hurry, Vanessa’s heels clicking down the walkway like she couldn’t get out fast enough. Riley watched their taillights disappear, then closed the heavy front door and threw the deadbolt. The house felt bigger without them. Hollow.

Lucas was already dragging her toward the kitchen. “I saved you the corner piece. It’s basically all crust.”

They ate cold pizza on the living room floor while some cartoon about singing animals played too loud. Lucas talked with his mouth full, telling her about school and how Josh Parker said girls couldn’t be astronauts anymore and how Riley should come to career day and tell everyone she could beat up astronauts if she wanted.

She laughed despite herself. The sound surprised her. She didn’t laugh much.

After dinner she let him win two games of Go Fish, then carried him upstairs piggyback while he waved Rex like a battle standard. His room smelled like fabric softener and the faint strawberry of kids’ toothpaste. She read him three chapters of *Captain Underpants*, doing all the voices the way he liked, until his eyelids started drooping.

“Miss Riley?” he said, voice already thick with sleep.

“Yeah, buddy?”

“Do you think bad men are real?”

The question landed like a stone in still water. She kept her face calm, brushing the hair out of his eyes.

“Some men are bad,” she said carefully. “But that’s why there are people who stop them.”

“Like police?”

“Sometimes.”

He seemed to think about that. “You’d stop them, right? If they came here?”

Riley’s right hand flexed, knuckles cracking softly in the quiet room. She forced it to stop.

“I’d keep you safe, Lucas. That’s what matters. Now go to sleep.”

She left his door cracked the way he liked and went downstairs. The house was too quiet. She walked from room to room checking windows, not sure why her stomach felt tight. Everything was locked. Everything looked normal.

At 9:12 her phone buzzed on the kitchen counter. Unknown number. She almost didn’t answer.

“Hello?”

Breathing. Then a man’s voice, low and rough. “Is this the Miller residence?”

“You have the wrong number,” she said automatically.

“No I don’t. Put Derek on.”

“He’s not here. Try his cell.”

The man laughed once, short and ugly. “Tell him the Bull says his time’s up. Tell him we know where his kid sleeps.”

The line went dead.

Riley stood very still in the middle of the expensive kitchen, phone still pressed to her ear. The cartoon animals were still singing faintly from the living room TV. Her heart was beating steady and slow, the way it used to before a fight behind the school bleachers all those years ago.

She walked to the knife block and pulled out the longest one, testing its weight. Then she went to the utility drawer and took out the claw hammer. She laid both on the marble island like surgical tools.

Upstairs, Lucas made a small sound in his sleep.

Riley cracked the knuckles on her right hand. Four times this time.

“Ordinary Tuesday,” she whispered to the empty house.

She moved to the front window and peered through the blinds. A dark SUV had parked across the street that wasn’t there when she arrived. Two men stood beside it, looking at the house. One of them checked his watch, just like Derek did when he was nervous.

Riley let the blinds fall closed.

Her voice, when it came, was quiet. Almost gentle.

“They fucked with the wrong babysitter.”

She picked up the hammer.

# Chapter 2: Something Feels Wrong

Riley stood in the darkened kitchen with the hammer in her right hand and the phone still warm in her left. The cartoon from the living room had ended; now the TV played some infomercial on low volume, a man promising perfect abs in thirty days. The house felt suddenly enormous, every creak of the settling foundation loud as a footstep.

Lucas was asleep upstairs. That was the only fact that mattered.

She moved through the first floor like a ghost, bare feet silent on the cold tile. Checked the sliding glass door to the backyard—locked. The windows in the dining room—locked. She paused at the front door, listening. Nothing but the hum of the refrigerator and her own breathing. Still, the skin on the back of her neck wouldn’t stop crawling.

The man on the phone hadn’t sounded like he was bluffing.

She climbed the stairs two at a time, avoiding the third step that always squeaked. Lucas’s door was still cracked. She pushed it open gently. He was curled on his side, Rex the dinosaur tucked under his chin, thumb half in his mouth. His breathing was soft and even. For a moment she let herself just watch him. Seven years old and already learning that the world wasn’t safe. She remembered being that small. Remembered her father’s belt. Remembered the boy behind the bleachers who thought she was easy prey.

Her hand tightened on the hammer.

She left his door open a little wider and went to the guest bedroom at the end of the hall where she sometimes slept if the Millers came home too late. From the top shelf of the closet she pulled down an old metal lunchbox she’d stashed there months ago. Inside: a cheap prepaid phone, a folding knife, thirty dollars in twenties, and a spare set of car keys. She slipped the knife into her hoodie pocket. The weight felt familiar. Dangerous.

Back in the hallway she froze.

The power flickered.

The hallway nightlight stuttered once, twice, then died. The whole house plunged into darkness except for the faint blue glow of the TV downstairs. Riley’s breath caught. She counted to ten in her head. When the lights didn’t come back, she moved.

She found the circuit breaker in the utility closet. Everything looked normal. No tripped switches. She flipped the main breaker off and on anyway. Nothing. Someone had cut the power from outside.

“Shit,” she whispered.

Lucas’s voice drifted from his room, small and scared. “Miss Riley?”

“I’m here, buddy.” She kept her voice light as she walked back to him. “Power went out. No big deal. Stay in bed, okay?”

He sat up, clutching Rex. “Is it the bad men?”

Her stomach twisted. “What bad men, Lucas?”

He looked down at his dinosaur, ashamed. “Daddy said not to tell. He said some men might come looking for money and I should hide in the closet and be really quiet until they go away.”

Riley felt something cold settle in her chest. She crouched beside the bed so their faces were level. “When did he tell you that?”

“Last week. After he yelled at Mommy.” Lucas’s lower lip trembled. “He said it was a secret game. But I don’t like this game.”

She brushed the hair out of his eyes. Her hand was shaking. “It’s not a game. But I’m not gonna let anything happen to you. Understand?”

He nodded, eyes wide.

She pulled the comforter off the bed. “We’re gonna make a fort in your closet. Like a superhero base. You and Rex can hide in there if you need to. Sound good?”

He nodded again, smaller this time.

While Lucas arranged his pillows and Rex inside the closet, Riley dragged the heavy wooden dresser in front of the bedroom door. It scraped loudly against the hardwood. She winced. The sound would carry. She stacked two chairs on top of the dresser for good measure, then checked the windows. The backyard was pitch black. No streetlights. No moon.

Her prepaid phone had no signal. Of course it didn’t.

She sat on the floor beside the closet, hammer across her lap, listening. The house made small noises—pipes ticking, wind against the eaves. Every one of them sounded like footsteps.

A memory flashed, uninvited. Her father’s voice in the trailer outside Fort Bragg, thick with beer: *You hit first, Riley. You hit hardest. World don’t give a shit if you’re small.* She’d been nine. She remembered the crack of her fist against the heavy bag until her knuckles split. She remembered the boy at school whose nose she’d broken so badly they had to wire his jaw shut. She remembered the look on the judge’s face when he called her “a danger to herself and others.”

She cracked her knuckles again. Once. Twice.

Downstairs, glass shattered.

The sound was sharp, unmistakable. A window breaking in the kitchen. Riley was on her feet before she realized she’d moved. Lucas whimpered from inside the closet.

“Stay there,” she whispered. “Don’t come out no matter what you hear. Promise me.”

A small voice: “Promise.”

She left the bedroom door cracked behind her and crept down the hall. The stairs felt endless. At the bottom she pressed herself against the wall, hammer raised. Cold air drifted from the kitchen. The sliding door was open now, curtain billowing like a ghost.

Two shapes moved in the darkness. Big men. One carried a flashlight, the beam cutting across the living room. The other had something in his hand that caught the light—a gun.

“Kid’s upstairs,” the one with the flashlight muttered. “Boss said make it quick. Grab the boy, leave the note on the kitchen table. Miller’ll pay up once he sees we got his spawn.”

The second man chuckled. “What about the babysitter?”

“Take her out if she screams. Or don’t. Nobody gives a shit about the help.”

Riley felt the switch flip inside her chest. That old familiar click. The one that had put a boy in the hospital when she was fifteen. The one she’d spent six years trying to bury.

She stepped into the kitchen.

The men turned. The flashlight beam hit her full in the face. She didn’t flinch.

“You’re early,” she said quietly.

The man with the gun laughed. “Jesus, it’s the fucking babysitter. Go back to bed, sweetheart. This ain’t your problem.”

Riley’s grip tightened on the hammer. Her voice came out flat. Almost bored.

“You broke the window.”

The first man took a step forward, still smiling. “Yeah? What are you gonna do about it, little girl?”

She moved.

The hammer came up fast and ugly, catching him across the temple with a wet crack. He dropped like someone had cut his strings. The flashlight rolled across the tile, throwing wild shadows.

The second man raised his gun, eyes wide with sudden shock. “What the fu—”

Riley was already inside his reach. She drove the hammer into his elbow. The gun clattered away. He screamed. She hit him again, this time in the jaw. Something broke. He staggered back against the counter, eyes wide with disbelief.

She stood over the first man, chest heaving, hammer dripping.

Upstairs, Lucas started to cry.

The second intruder groaned, trying to push himself up. Blood ran from his split lip. “You crazy bitch. You have no idea who you’re messing with.”

Riley looked down at him. Her hazel eyes were very calm.

“I think I’m starting to get the picture,” she said.

She raised the hammer again.

From somewhere outside came the sound of car doors slamming. More of them.

Riley’s right hand cracked once against her thigh.

“Stay down,” she told the man bleeding on her floor. “Or don’t. Your choice.”

She turned and ran for the stairs, leaving bloody footprints behind her.

She cracked her knuckles. Four times.

Riley didn’t smile back.

The Bull screamed as it hit his face and eyes. He staggered, clawing at his skin. She was already moving down the stairs toward him, garrote stretched between her hands.

This house was theirs tonight.

He let her pick him up. His small body was rigid at first, then melted against her as she carried him down the stairs, stepping carefully over the dead and unconscious men. He hid his face in her neck so he wouldn’t have to see.

Outside the night air was cold. The dark SUV the crew had arrived in sat idling at the curb, driver’s door open. Riley put Lucas in the back seat and buckled him in tight. She found a blanket in the trunk and wrapped it around him. Then she went back inside one last time.

She stood in the ruined kitchen and looked at the mess she’d made. The bloody hammer. The broken glass. The bodies. She felt something inside her chest crack open and bleed. This was not who she wanted to be. But it was who she had become the second they put their hands on Lucas.

She picked up the prepaid phone she’d taken from the Bull and dialed 911. When the operator answered she spoke fast and flat.

“Miller residence. Multiple intruders. Some of them are dead. The rest are breathing. Send police and an ambulance. The little boy is safe. That’s all you need to know.”

She left the phone on the counter and walked out without looking back.

The SUV smelled like cigarettes and cheap cologne. Riley climbed behind the wheel, wincing as the cut on her ribs pulled. She was losing too much blood. Her vision kept blurring at the edges. She adjusted the rearview mirror so she could see Lucas.

“You okay back there?”

He wouldn’t look at her. “I want my mom and dad.”

“I know, buddy. Me too. But right now it’s just us.”

She put the SUV in drive and pulled away from the house. In the rearview mirror the big suburban McMansion looked smaller. Innocent. Like nothing terrible had happened inside it.

They drove in silence for ten minutes. Lucas finally spoke, voice tiny.

“Are you going to hurt more people?”

Riley’s hands tightened on the wheel until her scarred knuckles went white. She cracked them once against the steering wheel. The sound made Lucas flinch.

“I don’t want to,” she said honestly. “But they were going to take you. They were going to hurt you to make your dad pay money. I can’t let that happen.”

Lucas was quiet for so long she thought he’d fallen asleep. Then he said, “You sounded scary. Like you liked it.”

The truth of it sat heavy in her stomach. She had liked it. Some part of her had liked the way the hammer felt when it landed. The way the men had looked at her with sudden fear instead of amusement. The babysitter they thought they could ignore.

She swallowed hard.

“I’m sorry you saw that.”

She drove toward the edge of town, heading for the only place she could think of: her own shitty apartment complex on the south side. She kept one hand on the wheel and the other pressed to her bleeding side. The SUV’s heater blasted hot air that smelled like exhaust.

Halfway there Lucas spoke again.

“Miss Riley?”

“Yeah?”

“If you’re not you anymore… who are you?”

The question lodged in her throat like a bone. She didn’t have an answer. The girl who read bedtime stories and the girl who crushed skulls with a hammer felt like two different people who happened to wear the same skin.

She pulled into the parking lot of her apartment building and killed the engine. The complex was quiet. No lights on in most windows. She turned in her seat to look at Lucas. He looked so small wrapped in that blanket, Rex clutched to his chest.

“I’m the person who’s going to keep you alive,” she said. “Even if it means I stop being nice. Can you be okay with that for tonight?”

He thought about it. Then he nodded once, very small.

She helped him out of the car. Her legs felt weak. The cut on her side had soaked through the hoodie and was now dripping down her jeans. She needed to stitch it. She needed antibiotics. She needed to stop bleeding everywhere.

But first she needed to arm herself properly.

She left Lucas in the front seat with the doors locked while she popped the trunk of her own ancient Corolla. Inside the spare tire compartment she kept a small go-bag she hadn’t touched in three years. Inside it: a cheap 9mm she’d bought off a guy in juvie, two magazines, a folding knife, zip ties, and a bottle of painkillers. She stared at the gun for a long moment before she took it.

This was it. The point of no return.

She slipped the gun into her waistband, zipped the hoodie over it, and walked back to the stolen SUV. Lucas watched her through the window with wide, frightened eyes.

Riley climbed into the driver’s seat and looked at her own reflection in the rearview mirror. Blood on her face. Hair wild. Eyes too bright, too empty.

She cracked the knuckles on her right hand slowly, one by one.

“No more hiding,” she whispered to the girl in the mirror.

Then she started the engine and pulled out of the parking lot, heading back toward the city with a stolen gun, a bleeding side, and a seven-year-old boy who was starting to fear her almost as much as the bad men.

The babysitter was gone.

Something else was driving now.

# Chapter 6: Following the Thread

The stolen SUV smelled like blood and bleach. Riley drove with one hand on the wheel and the other pressed hard against the gash in her side. The pain had settled into a deep, throbbing burn that matched the rhythm of her heartbeat. Lucas sat in the back, wrapped in the blanket, staring at her in the rearview mirror like she was a stranger wearing his babysitter’s face.

She cracked her right knuckles against the steering wheel. Four times. The sound made Lucas flinch again.

“You’re bleeding on the seat,” he said quietly.

“I know.”

“Are you gonna die?”

“Not tonight.”

She popped two of the painkillers from her go-bag and dry-swallowed them. They tasted like chalk and regret. The gun in her waistband pressed cold against her spine. She hadn’t carried one in three years. It felt like cheating. Like admitting the girl who tried to be good had lost.

The flip phone she’d taken off the Bull buzzed in the cupholder. Unknown number. She answered on speaker.

A calm voice filled the car. “You got my guys?”

Riley glanced at Lucas in the mirror. He had Rex pressed to his mouth.

“Yeah,” she said. “Most of them. Your boss is taking a nap in the hallway. Permanent one.”

A long pause. Then a low chuckle that made her skin crawl.

“Well, shit. The babysitter. Marco said you were supposed to be some tiny nothing. Guess he was wrong.” The man on the phone sounded almost impressed. “You got balls, girl. I’ll give you that.”

“What do you want?” Riley asked. Her voice was flat. The painkillers were starting to blur the edges of everything.

“I want my money. Sixty grand your boss owes me. You bring me the kid, I’ll let you walk. Hell, I’ll even pay you for the trouble. Ten grand. Cash. No hard feelings.”

Riley laughed. The sound came out ugly and wet. “Hard feelings? You sent men to grab a seven-year-old. You broke into his house. You touched him. There’s nothing but hard feelings.”

In the back seat Lucas made a small sound.

The voice on the phone hardened. “Then we got a problem. Because I got four more guys and you got one little boy and a hole in your side. I can hear it in your breathing, sweetheart. You’re hurting.”

Riley’s grip tightened until the wheel creaked. She looked at Lucas again. He was crying silently now, tears rolling down his cheeks.

“Tell me where you are,” she said.

The man laughed. “You think I’m stupid?”

“No. I think you’re arrogant. And I think you’re starting to realize the tiny babysitter just put down six of your crew. So tell me where you are, or I start calling every cop in the city and giving them your name.”

Another pause. She could almost hear him recalculating.

“Fine,” he said. “Strip mall on the east side. Vacant office behind the laundromat. Unit 14B. You got twenty minutes before I send the rest of the boys to finish what they started. And babysitter? If the kid’s hurt when you get here, I’m gonna make you watch while I take it out on you slow.”

The line went dead.

Riley drove faster.

The painkillers were kicking in hard now, making the streetlights smear across her vision. She kept one eye on the rearview mirror. Lucas had gone very quiet.

“Miss Riley,” he said after a while. “That man on the phone. He sounded scared of you.”

“Good.”

“Are you scared of you?”

She didn’t answer.

The strip mall was a dying strip of 1970s concrete on the bad side of town. The laundromat was still open, fluorescent lights buzzing over rows of machines. Unit 14B was dark, the metal door dented like someone had kicked it a lot. Riley parked two spaces down and killed the engine.

She turned to Lucas. “I need you to do something hard for me.”

He nodded, eyes wide.

“Stay in the car. Doors locked. If anyone but me comes to the window, you duck down and hold Rex tight and don’t make a sound. If I’m not back in ten minutes, you use this phone—” she handed him the Bull’s flip phone “—and call 911. Tell them everything. Can you do that?”

His lip trembled. “I don’t want you to go.”

“I know.” She reached back and squeezed his knee. Her hand left a faint bloody print on the blanket. “But this is the only way I can make sure they never come after you again. I have to finish it.”

She climbed out of the SUV before he could argue. The night air was cold against her clammy skin. She zipped the hoodie all the way up to hide the blood, tucked the gun into the front of her waistband where she could reach it fast, and walked toward the laundromat like a tired young woman who just wanted clean clothes.

Inside, the place was empty except for an old woman folding towels in the corner. Riley nodded at her like nothing was wrong. The woman stared at the blood on her jeans but said nothing. People in this neighborhood had learned not to ask questions.

Riley slipped out the back exit that led to the service alley. Unit 14B had a rear door with a broken security light. Perfect.

She pressed herself against the brick wall and listened. Two voices inside. One calm, one nervous. The calm one had been on the phone. She recognized the cadence.

“...says she’s on her way. Crazy bitch actually thinks she can take us. After what she did to the Bull? I want her alive. I’m gonna make an example.”

The nervous one laughed too loud. “She’s five foot nothing, man. We got guns.”

Riley took a slow breath. Then she kicked the door so hard the cheap lock ripped out of the frame.

She stepped inside with the gun raised.

Two men. The one behind the desk was older, maybe fifty, with a face like a retired boxer and a nasty scar across his left cheek. The nervous one was younger, maybe twenty-five, holding a shotgun like he didn’t quite know what to do with it.

They both looked up in surprise.

The older one—had to be the boss—actually smiled. “Well, fuck me. You really did show up.”

Riley shot the younger one in the knee.

The shotgun went off as he fell, blowing a hole in the ceiling. Plaster rained down. The older man reached for the pistol on the desk but froze when Riley swung the gun toward him.

“Don’t,” she said.

He raised his hands slowly. His eyes flicked over her bloody clothes, the way she was listing slightly to the left, the absolute lack of fear in her face.

“You’re not what I expected,” he said.

“You neither. I thought you’d be taller.”

He chuckled like they were at a bar trading jokes. “Name’s Vic. Vic Salazar. Your boss owes me a lot of money, little girl. Sixty large. Plus interest now that you killed half my crew.”

Riley stepped closer. The gun didn’t waver. “His name is Derek Miller and he’s a piece of shit. But that little boy in the car? He’s not. He’s just a kid who likes dinosaurs and thinks his babysitter is supposed to keep him safe. You came after the wrong person when you came after him.”

Vic studied her. Something shifted in his expression. “You’re not doing this for money.”

“No.”

“You’re hurt bad. I can see it. You’re running on fumes and spite. Put the gun down and we can talk. Maybe we both walk away.”

Riley’s hand was steady. The pain in her side had gone distant, like it belonged to someone else.

“I’m done talking.”

She made him get on his knees. Made him tell her everything—how much Derek owed, who else was involved, where the rest of the crew would be waiting. Every time he hesitated she pressed the gun against his forehead harder. When he finally ran out of words she zip-tied his hands behind his back with the ties from her go-bag.

Then she crouched in front of him so they were eye level.

“You sent men to grab a seven-year-old,” she said quietly. “You told them to take him if his parents didn’t pay. You told them the babysitter didn’t matter.” She cracked her bloody knuckles slowly. “I matter.”

Vic’s cocky smile was gone now. Real fear had finally settled in his eyes.

“What are you gonna do?” he asked.

Riley stood up. The room tilted slightly. She was losing too much blood. She needed to finish this and get Lucas somewhere safe.

“I’m going to send your boss a message,” she said.

She picked up the hammer she’d carried from the house. It felt heavier than before.

When she walked out of the office ten minutes later, her hoodie was wetter than when she’d gone in. She left Vic alive. Barely. The word “BABYSITTER” was carved across his chest in jagged letters. Crude. Ugly. Personal.

She climbed back into the SUV. Lucas was crying quietly in the back seat.

“Miss Riley,” he whispered when he saw the fresh blood. “You’re scarier than the bad men.”

She started the engine. Her hands left red prints on the wheel.

“I know,” she said.

She drove away from the laundromat with the taste of copper in her mouth and the growing certainty that the girl who used to read bedtime stories was never coming back.

The thread was pulled tight now.

And it was leading straight to Derek and Vanessa Miller.

# Chapter 7: The Parents Get What They Deserve

Riley’s hands left red smears on the steering wheel as she drove. The painkillers had worn off and the gash in her side felt like someone was digging a hot poker between her ribs with every breath. Lucas had stopped crying. He just sat in the back seat now, staring at her with wide, exhausted eyes, Rex clutched tight like a shield.

The flip phone buzzed again. She answered without looking.

A woman’s voice this time. Vanessa.

“Riley? Oh God, Riley is that you? The house—there’s police everywhere. They said there were bodies. They said—”

“Shut up.” Riley’s voice was raw. “Where are you?”

A pause. Then Derek’s voice came on, shaky. “We’re at the Starlight Motel off the highway. Room 19. Riley, listen, we can explain—”

“No. You listen. I’m bringing your son to you. And you’re going to fix what you broke. Both of you. Or I swear to God I will finish what those men started.”

She hung up before they could answer.

The Starlight Motel was the kind of place people went when they didn’t want to be found. Peeling pink stucco, buzzing neon sign missing half its letters. Riley parked the stolen SUV two doors down from Room 19 and sat for a moment with her eyes closed. The gun in her waistband felt heavier than before. So did the guilt.

Lucas spoke from the back seat, voice barely above a whisper. “Are Mommy and Daddy going to be mad at you?”

She cracked her right knuckles against the dashboard. The sound was weaker now. “They can be mad at me all they want. As long as you’re safe.”

She helped him out of the car. He didn’t want to hold her hand anymore. He walked a half-step behind her, like he was scared of what she might do next. That hurt worse than the bleeding.

Riley knocked on the door of Room 19 with the hand that wasn’t holding her side together. The door opened immediately.

Vanessa stood there in yesterday’s clothes, makeup smudged, hair wild. When she saw Lucas she let out a sound that was half sob, half relief and dropped to her knees, arms open. Lucas ran to her and buried his face in her chest. For the first time all night Riley felt like an outsider looking in.

Then Derek appeared behind his wife. His expensive haircut was wrecked. His eyes widened when he took in Riley—bloody, pale, swaying slightly in the doorway.

“Jesus Christ,” he breathed. “What the hell happened to you?”

Riley pushed past them into the room and closed the door. The place smelled like old cigarettes and desperation. One sad lamp. Two queen beds. A half-empty bottle of vodka on the nightstand.

She leaned against the wall so she wouldn’t fall over.

“You happened to me,” she said. Her voice was quiet but every word landed like a hammer. “You and your sixty thousand dollar mistake. They came for Lucas. They put their hands on him. They told me the babysitter didn’t matter.”

Vanessa looked up from where she was clutching Lucas. Her perfectly frozen face had finally cracked. “We didn’t know they’d come tonight. We thought we had more time—”

“Time?” Riley laughed once, a harsh bark that made her wince. “You left your seven-year-old son with me while you went to some shady meeting. You knew something was wrong. You told him to hide in the closet if bad men came. You knew.”

Derek tried to sound reasonable. “Look, Riley, we can pay you. Double your normal rate. Triple. Just… help us get out of this. We can go to the police together. You’re the hero here. You saved our son.”

Riley’s eyes went flat.

She pulled the gun from her waistband.

Both parents froze.

“I’m not your hero,” she said. “I’m the girl you paid minimum wage to protect the one good thing in your shitty lives. And I had to become something else to do it. I had to break people. I had to break myself.”

Lucas was watching her again. That same scared look. She hated it.

She lowered the gun but didn’t put it away.

“You’re going to call your boss. The one who sent those men. You’re going to tell him you have the money and you want to meet. Tonight. You’re going to take me with you. And you’re going to tell him the babysitter is the one who wants to talk.”

Derek’s face went pale. “You don’t understand. Vic Salazar doesn’t negotiate. He’s—”

“Vic Salazar is zip-tied to a chair in a laundromat office with my name carved in his chest,” Riley said calmly. “He’s not going to be a problem.”

Vanessa made a small choking sound.

Derek stared at her like he was seeing her for the first time. “Who the hell are you?”

Riley gave him a tired, ugly smile. “I’m the babysitter. And you fucked with the wrong one.”

She made them call Salazar’s second-in-command. Derek’s hands shook so badly he could barely dial. Riley stood close enough to hear both sides of the conversation. The meeting was set for forty minutes from now at an abandoned self-storage facility on the outskirts of town. Neutral ground, supposedly. Riley knew better.

While they waited she let Vanessa clean the worst of the blood off her face and tape a makeshift bandage over the knife wound. The woman’s hands trembled the entire time.

“You really killed all those men?” Vanessa whispered while Lucas was in the bathroom.

Riley looked at her. Really looked. “Some of them. The ones who touched your son. The ones who laughed about hurting him. Yeah. I did.”

Vanessa swallowed. “I’m sorry. We never meant for any of this to touch Lucas. Or you.”

“Sorry doesn’t mean much when you’re bleeding in someone else’s house.”

When Lucas came back out he wouldn’t look at Riley. He stayed glued to his mother’s side. That hurt more than the wound.

Derek paced the room, checking his watch every twenty seconds like always. “This is insane. We should just run. Take the cash we have and disappear.”

“You’re not running,” Riley said. “Not until this is finished. Lucas doesn’t get to grow up looking over his shoulder because his parents are cowards.”

The words came out harsher than she meant. Lucas flinched.

She softened her voice as much as she could. “Hey. Monster.”

He looked at her reluctantly.

“I’m still your Miss Riley,” she said. “Even if I’m scary right now. Even if I have to do scary things. I’m doing them for you. Okay?”

He didn’t answer. But he gave one tiny nod.

They left the motel in the stolen SUV. Derek drove. Vanessa sat in the passenger seat. Riley sat in the back with Lucas, the gun resting on her lap under the blanket. Every bump in the road sent fresh pain through her side. She was starting to feel cold. That was a bad sign.

As they got closer to the storage facility, Derek kept glancing at her in the rearview mirror.

“You’re not going to let us just hand over the money and walk away, are you?” he asked.

Riley met his eyes in the mirror. Her hazel eyes looked almost black in the dashboard light.

“No,” she said simply. “I’m not.”

Vanessa started crying quietly. Derek’s knuckles were white on the steering wheel.

Riley cracked her right hand knuckles one last time. The sound was soft. Tired.

She looked down at Lucas, who had finally fallen into an exhausted sleep with his head against her arm, Rex still clutched in his small fist.

She brushed a strand of hair from his forehead with fingers that left a faint bloody streak on his temple.

“I’m sorry you had to see what I really am,” she whispered to the sleeping boy.

Then she looked up at the dark road ahead.

The final stop was coming.

And this time the parents weren’t going to hide behind the babysitter.
