# Jack Moss

**Background, personality, idiosyncrasies, flaws**  
Jack Moss is 38, a former vice cop who spent eight years working the city’s queer underground bars and clubs before the department quietly forced him out after he refused to keep shaking down the same people he sometimes slept with. He now runs a one-man PI operation out of a damp second-floor office above a Chinese laundry. He drinks too much but never before noon (a rule he breaks more often than he admits).  

Personality: dry, self-mocking, observant to the point of cruelty, especially toward himself. He has a habit of narrating his own stupidity in real time. Idiosyncrasies include always carrying two lighters (one for himself, one he pretends to lose so strangers will ask him for a light), collecting matchbooks from every bar he drinks in, and keeping an old Polaroid of his mother in his wallet even though she died when he was twelve. Flaws: chronic commitment issues, a vicious streak when cornered, and a tendency to romanticize his own loneliness. He tells himself he’s “done with people” while secretly hoping someone will prove him wrong. Trivial example: he refuses to buy new socks and will wear the same pair until the heel is completely gone; he claims it’s about thrift but it’s really about hating small domestic tasks.

**Physicality**  
Medium height, broad through the shoulders from years of carrying the weight of the job. Dark hair that’s starting to gray at the temples; he keeps it short because he can’t be bothered. A faint scar through his left eyebrow from a bar fight he doesn’t talk about. He carries himself like a man who expects to be hit—loose but ready, hands usually in his coat pockets. When he smokes, he does it with religious focus, eyes half-lidded, watching the smoke like it’s telling him secrets. His voice is low and a little rough, like he’s been shouting at the rain for years.

**Motives, allegiances, existing relationships**  
Jack wants to be left alone almost as much as he wants to be wanted. He took the job tracking Luca because the money was good and because the club owner who hired him used to be one of his informants. His only real allegiance is to his own survival, yet he keeps getting pulled back into other people’s messes. He has a toxic on-again-off-again history with Detective Frank Reyes—his former partner and occasional lover—who represents both safety and betrayal. Jack doesn’t trust Reyes, but he also can’t quite quit him. Deep down he knows he’s looking for an excuse to burn his own life down again.

**Voice examples**  
Internal monologue: “He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas, and I was standing there with a lighter like a goddamn idiot.”  

Dialogue: “Look, kid, I’ve met trouble before. Trouble usually doesn’t smile like that. Makes me nervous.”

# Luca Vale

**Background, personality, idiosyncrasies, flaws**  
Luca is 29, born in the city’s decaying Italian quarter. He ran away from home at sixteen after his father caught him with another boy and beat him so badly he still has a slight hitch in his left shoulder when it rains. He has survived by being beautiful, useful, and disposable in equal measure—singing in clubs, running small cons, occasionally selling himself when the rent came due. He stole the ledger on impulse after one of the men in it roughed him up; now he’s in way over his head and pretending he isn’t.

Personality: magnetic, restless, funny in a mean way, allergic to sincerity. He treats lying like breathing. Idiosyncrasies: he steals small things constantly (lighters, pens, someone’s last cigarette) not because he needs them but because it gives him a tiny sense of control. He hums old jazz standards when he’s nervous. Flaws: he is pathologically unable to tell the truth even when it would save him; he panics and lashes out when people get too close; he has a self-destructive streak that makes him push away anyone who might actually care. Trivial example: he always orders his whiskey neat but then lets the ice from other people’s drinks melt into it because he likes the way it tastes after someone else has been drinking it.

**Physicality**  
Slim but wiry, with the kind of careless grace that makes people watch him cross a room. Sharp cheekbones, dark eyes that look almost black in low light, a mouth that looks like it was made for lying and other bad ideas. He dresses like he doesn’t care—slightly oversized shirts, worn leather jacket two sizes too big, scuffed boots—but somehow it always looks intentional. He moves like smoke himself: quiet, drifting, gone before you realize he’s left. When he smokes he lets the ash grow dangerously long, daring it to fall.

**Motives, allegiances, existing relationships**  
Luca’s primary motive is survival, followed closely by not being bored. He stole the ledger both for money and because he was angry; now he’s half-looking for someone to sell it to and half-looking for someone to save him from it. He has no real allegiances except to himself, though he feels an inconvenient flicker of guilt about dragging Jack into his mess. He has a complicated, semi-familial relationship with the owner of The Velvet Room (the club that hired Jack), who once gave him a place to sleep when he was seventeen. He and Reyes have never met but Luca has heard enough to know the man is dangerous. Deep down Luca is exhausted by his own games but doesn’t know how to stop playing them.

**Voice examples**  
Internal monologue: “Another good man with sad eyes. Christ, I really am a cliché.”  

Dialogue: “You gonna arrest me or kiss me, Detective? Clock’s ticking and I only got one cigarette left.”

# Frank Reyes

**Background, personality, idiosyncrasies, flaws**  
Frank Reyes is 42, still a detective on the force, the man who taught Jack how to look the other way and then hated him for learning the lesson too well. He grew up hard in the same neighborhood as Luca but chose the badge instead of the street. He is married (to a woman who doesn’t ask questions) and has two kids he barely sees. He keeps Jack’s old precinct mug in his desk drawer like a penance and a threat.

Personality: controlled, quietly vicious, charismatic when he needs to be. He smiles with his mouth but not his eyes. Idiosyncrasies: he always polishes his badge before a dirty job; he drinks his coffee black but puts three sugars in when he’s stressed. Flaws: jealous, possessive, fundamentally hypocritical—he sleeps with men but punishes others for the same thing. He genuinely believes he’s the hero of his own story. Trivial example: he clips coupons from the newspaper even though he makes decent money; he hates wasting anything, including people.

**Physicality**  
Tall, solid, ex-boxer build. Neatly trimmed mustache, hair always perfectly combed. He wears slightly too-tight suits that show off the fact he still works out. His hands are large and surprisingly gentle until they’re not. He moves with deliberate authority, taking up space like he owns it.

**Motives, allegiances, existing relationships**  
Reyes wants the ledger because it contains photographs of him with several men, including Jack. He is allied with the crime boss who wants the ledger back for his own protection. His relationship with Jack is toxic nostalgia mixed with genuine resentment; he both wants Jack back under his thumb and wants to punish him for leaving the force. He sees Luca as an annoying loose end that needs cutting.

**Voice examples**  
Internal monologue: “Jack never could resist a pretty disaster. That’s how I got him in the first place.”  

Dialogue: “You always did have shit taste in men, Moss. This one’s gonna get you killed. Try not to enjoy it too much.”

The rain was doing that thing it always does in this city—coming down sideways, like it’s got a personal grudge. I sat behind my desk with the lights off, watching the neon from the laundry sign bleed across the window in runny pinks and blues. The office smelled like wet wool, stale coffee, and the ghost of last night’s cigarettes. My own pack was almost empty. Story of my goddamn life.

The phone rang at ten past nine. I let it ring three times before I picked up, because some habits die harder than others.

“Moss.”

The voice on the other end belonged to Teddy Marino, owner of The Velvet Room, the kind of underground club where the boys danced close and the girls in suits bought the drinks. Teddy didn’t waste time with pleasantries. “There’s a kid. Name’s Luca Vale. Used to work for me. Host, singer, pretty face, big mouth. He lifted something that doesn’t belong to him. A ledger. I need it back before the wrong people notice it’s gone.”

I rubbed the scar through my eyebrow. “How much?”

“Fifteen hundred. Plus expenses. And discretion, Jack. The kind you used to be good at.”

I should’ve said no. The rain was telling me to say no. My liver was telling me to say no. But fifteen hundred would cover the rent for three months and the bottle of decent bourbon I’d been eyeing. I heard myself say yes anyway.

“Last seen?”

“Blue Note, two nights ago. Looking twitchy. You know the place.”

I knew it. Knew the sticky floors and the way the smoke hung low enough to taste. I also knew Teddy wasn’t telling me the whole story. Nobody ever does.

“Give me forty-eight hours before you send anyone else,” I said.

Teddy laughed like a man who’d already sent someone else. “Clock’s running, Moss.”

I hung up, lit my second-to-last cigarette, and stared at the rain some more. He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas, the voice in my head whispered, even though I hadn’t even seen the kid yet. I hated when my own brain started writing noir for me.

The Blue Note was downtown, wedged between a pawn shop and a boarded-up theater. I pushed through the door a little after eleven. The place was half-full: tired queens nursing warm beers, a scattering of rough boys looking for trouble, and one tired bartender polishing the same glass he’d been polishing since Truman was president.

I ordered a whiskey, left it untouched, and scanned the room.

He was in the far corner booth, alone, like he’d reserved the solitude. The first thing I noticed was the smoke. It curled up from the cigarette between his long fingers like it was part of him, wrapping around his throat, sliding across his sharp cheekbones, drifting past lips that looked like they’d been designed by someone with very poor judgment. Dark hair fell across his forehead in careless waves. Leather jacket two sizes too big. When he lifted the cigarette to his mouth again, ash tumbled onto the table and he didn’t bother brushing it away.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

I felt it low in my gut, that stupid electric click. The one that says *walk away, Moss. Just turn around and walk away.* Instead I picked up my untouched whiskey and crossed the room.

He looked up as I approached. Eyes so dark they swallowed the neon. There was a split second where something flickered across his face—recognition, maybe fear, maybe just the calculation of how much trouble I represented—then it smoothed into a lazy smile.

“You’re in my light,” he said.

I sat down anyway. “Luca Vale?”

The smile didn’t waver but his fingers tightened minutely on the cigarette. “Depends who’s asking. You a cop?”

“Used to be. Now I’m just the guy Teddy sent.”

“Ah.” He took a long drag, held it, then let the smoke spill slowly from his mouth like he was performing for me. “Figured he’d send someone eventually. You don’t look like his usual muscle.”

“I’m not. I’m the guy who finds things.”

He studied me for a long moment. The jukebox kicked into an old Billie Holiday number, something about love being a losing game. Appropriate.

“Well, Jack Moss,” he said—because of course he knew my name already—“I don’t have the ledger on me. And even if I did, I’m not sure I’d give it to you.”

“I’m not here to strong-arm you. Yet.”

He laughed softly. The sound did something unwelcome to my insides. “Honest PI. That’s new. You any good at your job?”

“Depends on the day.”

Another drag. The ash was getting dangerously long again. “Today’s not looking great for you, then.”

I leaned forward, elbows on the sticky table. Close enough to smell him—cigarettes, cheap cologne, and something sharper underneath, like fear wearing aftershave. “The people who own that ledger aren’t the forgiving type. Whatever game you’re playing, it’s going to end with you floating in the river wearing concrete shoes.”

“Poetic.” He tapped the cigarette once. Ash finally fell, scattering across the scarred wood like gray snow. “But I’ve been in tighter spots.”

I didn’t believe him. His fingers were trembling just slightly. Not enough for most people to notice. I wasn’t most people.

“Let me buy you a drink,” I said.

He tilted his head. “You trying to get me drunk or get me talking?”

“Both. In that order.”

Luca smiled again, smaller this time. The kind of smile that made smart men do very stupid things. He stubbed out the cigarette with deliberate care, then stood up in one fluid motion. The leather jacket settled on his slim shoulders like it belonged there.

“Rain’s getting worse,” he said. “I like walking in it. You coming?”

I left my whiskey untouched and followed him out.

The rain hit us like a punishment. Luca didn’t seem to mind. He turned his face up to it, eyes closed for a second, water sliding down his temples. I pulled my coat collar up and tried not to stare at the way his wet shirt was starting to cling.

We walked two blocks in silence. Then he stopped under a flickering streetlamp, turned to me, and said, “You’re not going to leave me alone, are you?”

“Probably not.”

He stepped closer. Close enough that I could see the faint scar on his lower lip. Close enough to feel the heat coming off him despite the cold rain. His hand came up, slow, and he plucked the last cigarette from behind my ear where I sometimes tucked them.

“Got a light?”

I produced the lighter. When I flicked it, the flame lit up his face from below, all sharp angles and dark eyes and that mouth. He leaned in to catch the flame, our faces inches apart. The cigarette caught. He inhaled, then tilted his head back and blew the smoke up into the rain where it dissolved like a bad decision.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

I don’t know which one of us moved first. Maybe it was mutual. One second we were standing there in the rain, the next his mouth was on mine.

He tasted like smoke and rain and bad choices. His free hand fisted in my coat, pulling me closer. The kiss wasn’t gentle. It had teeth. When we broke apart he was breathing harder, eyes a little wild.

“Fuck,” he whispered. Then he smiled that terrible, beautiful smile. “That was a mistake.”

“Probably.”

He took one more drag, then pressed the cigarette between my lips like a gift. I accepted it. The filter was warm from his mouth.

“See you around, Jack Moss.”

He turned and walked away, hands in his pockets, shoulders loose like he hadn’t just upended both our lives. I stood there in the rain holding a cigarette that wasn’t mine, watching the smoke curl up from it in the downpour, and felt the first sick lurch of something that felt a lot like hunger.

I took a long drag. The smoke burned all the way down.

“Goddamn it,” I said to the empty street.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And I was apparently into that.

The Blue Note’s sister establishment was a place called The Sinkhole, an after-hours club tucked behind an unmarked door in the meatpacking district. You had to knock twice, wait, then knock once more while the rain hammered the alley like it was trying to wash the sin off the streets. I knew the bouncer—ex-marine named Carl who owed me for not turning him in years ago when he was running pills. He let me in with a grunt.

Inside, the air was thicker than the previous night’s smoke. Jazz saxophone wailed low and dirty from a corner stage. The crowd was the usual mix: men in suits looking for company that wouldn’t ask questions, queens in silk who could cut you with a glance, and a handful of dangerous boys nursing their secrets along with their drinks. The bar itself was a scarred length of mahogany that had seen better decades.

I spotted him almost immediately, because my eyes had apparently decided to make him their full-time job. Luca was at the far end of the bar, one elbow propped on the wood, nursing what looked like straight bourbon. The cigarette between his fingers sent lazy spirals upward, wrapping around his throat again like it had missed him. His hair was still damp from the rain, curling at the nape. That oversized leather jacket hung off one shoulder, and the shirt underneath clung in all the wrong—right—places.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas, and I was already walking toward him like a moth with a death wish.

I slid onto the stool next to him without asking. He didn’t look surprised. Just took a slow drag and let the smoke drift my way, like an invitation or a warning.

“Following me now?” His voice was low, amused, edged with something sharper. “That’s pathetic, even for a PI.”

“Teddy’s paying me to be pathetic,” I said. “You gonna make this easy or are we doing the dance?”

Luca turned his head, eyes meeting mine. Those dark irises caught the low neon—red bleeding into black—and for a second I forgot the job. His mouth quirked. “I don’t do easy, Jack. Where’s the fun in that?”

The bartender, a rail-thin guy with a handlebar mustache that looked painted on, set a glass in front of me without being asked. Same cheap whiskey as last night. I ignored it and focused on the way Luca’s fingers tapped the cigarette, ash growing long again. He never seemed to notice until it fell.

“Ledger,” I said. “Give it up, we both walk away richer and alive. Simple.”

He laughed, soft and mean. “Simple. That’s cute. You think any of this is simple?” He leaned in closer, close enough that I caught the scent of him again—cigarettes, that cheap cologne that somehow worked, and underneath it all, the faint tang of fear sweat. “That book’s got names, Jack. Dates. Pictures that could ruin half the city’s upstanding citizens. Including a few cops. You really want to hand that back to Teddy like a good dog?”

I felt my jaw tighten. Pictures. Of course. The kind that got men like us buried quietly. “Who’d you steal it from?”

Luca shrugged, stole the lighter from my coat pocket in one smooth motion like it was nothing. He flicked it open, lit his cigarette even though it was already burning, then pocketed the lighter with a grin. “Lighter thief,” he said, like it was a title. “Suits me better than singer these days.”

“Give it back.”

“The lighter or the ledger?”

“Both.”

He exhaled smoke directly at me, playful and infuriating. The sax player hit a low, wailing note that matched the twist in my gut. “Make me.”

The challenge hung there, stupid and electric. I should’ve grabbed him by the collar, dragged him outside, done the job Teddy paid for. Instead I sat there watching the smoke curl from his lips, thinking about how that mouth had felt in the rain the night before. Bad ideas stacked on bad ideas.

We talked in circles for the next twenty minutes. He dodged every question with a quip or a half-truth. Claimed the ledger was insurance, not theft. Said the boss—some heavy named Moretti—had it coming after he sent goons to rough up one of the club boys. Luca’s voice stayed light, but his free hand kept clenching and unclenching on the bar. Idiosyncrasy. Tell. I filed it away.

“You’re twitchy,” I said finally.

“You’re observant. Must be why Teddy picked you.” He stole my untouched whiskey, took a sip, then slid it back with a wink. “Tastes better after you’ve been staring at it like it insulted your mother.”

I rubbed my temple. The smoke was getting to me, or maybe it was him. “Look, kid—”

“Twenty-nine. Not a kid.”

“—whatever game this is, it ends bloody. I’ve seen the players. Moretti doesn’t fuck around, and neither does the cop he’s got in his pocket.”

Luca’s eyes flickered at that. “Which cop?”

“Doesn’t matter.”

“It does if it’s the one who used to fuck you.”

The words landed like a slap. I kept my face still, but he saw it anyway. That wicked mouth curved. “Small world, huh? Reyes has a reputation. Mean streak wider than his mustache.”

“Shut up about Reyes.”

“Touchy.” He leaned in again, voice dropping. “He warn you off me yet? Bet he did. Bet it made you want to find me even more. You always did have shit taste in men, Jack.”

I grabbed his wrist before I could think better of it. Not hard enough to bruise, but enough to feel the pulse jumping under his skin. His skin was warm, cigarette ash smudged on his fingers. “You don’t know me.”

“I know enough.” He didn’t pull away. Instead he turned his hand, interlaced our fingers loosely, like we were something soft. The contrast—his slim, quick fingers against my scarred knuckles—did something stupid to my chest. “I know you followed me last night. Kissed me like a man drowning. And here you are again, buying drinks you don’t touch, asking questions you already know the answers to. So tell me, Jack Moss. You here for the ledger or for me?”

The saxophone died down. The club noise swelled around us—laughter too loud, glasses clinking like breaking promises. I let go of his wrist but didn’t move back. “Both. And that’s the problem.”

Luca’s expression shifted, just for a second. Something almost like regret under the smirk. Then it was gone. He plucked the half-smoked cigarette from his own mouth and pressed it between my lips. The filter was damp from him. I took the drag, feeling the burn, tasting him on it.

“Bad habit,” he murmured.

“You or the smoking?”

He laughed again, genuine this time. The sound cracked something in me. Before I could stop myself, I caught the front of his jacket and pulled him off the stool. We stumbled out the side door into the alley, rain still sheeting down, turning the ground to greasy mirrors.

The door banged shut behind us. Luca backed up against the brick wall, eyes bright in the dim security light. “This the part where you rough me up for information?”

“Shut up.”

I kissed him instead. Harder than last night. Like punishment. He tasted like my stolen whiskey and his own cigarette, all smoke and bad ideas. His hands were in my hair, tugging, then sliding down to grip my coat. The kiss turned messy fast—teeth, tongues, the scrape of stubble. I pressed him harder against the wall, feeling the lean length of him, the way he arched into it like he was starving too.

He broke away first, breathing ragged. “Fuck, Jack. This is... this is a mistake.”

“Yeah, well, I’m full of them tonight.” My voice came out rougher than I liked.

Luca’s fingers fumbled in my pocket, came out with my last cigarette. He lit it with my stolen lighter, hands shaking just enough to show. He took one drag, then offered it to me. I accepted, our fingers brushing. The smoke curled up between us, mingling with the rain.

“I don’t have the ledger here,” he said quietly, almost honest for once. “But I know where it is. Safety deposit box. Tomorrow night, maybe we could—”

A car door slammed at the mouth of the alley. We both froze.

Reyes stepped out, coat collar up, badge glinting under the streetlight even though he wasn’t supposed to be flashing it in a place like this. His mustache was neat as ever, eyes cold. He looked at us—at me with my shirt half-untucked, at Luca still pinned to the wall like a guilty secret—and his mouth twisted.

“Jack,” he said, voice flat. “Didn’t take you long.”

Luca tensed under my hands. I stepped back, putting myself between them without thinking. “Frank. This isn’t your business.”

Reyes laughed once, short and ugly. “Everything’s my business when it involves that ledger. And you. Still chasing pretty disasters, I see.” His gaze flicked to Luca. “Vale. You’ve got twenty-four hours to hand it over before Moretti’s crew starts carving pieces off your friends at the Velvet Room. After that, I come for you myself. And Jack here won’t be able to save you. He never could save anyone, least of all himself.”

Luca’s face went blank, but his hand found the small of my back, a fleeting touch. Support or manipulation, I couldn’t tell.

Reyes looked at me one last time, something like old hurt flickering under the anger. “Walk away, Moss. Before this one gets you killed. You always did have shit taste.”

He got back in his car and drove off, taillights bleeding red into the rain.

The alley felt smaller after that. Luca exhaled shakily, stole the cigarette back from me, and took a long pull. “Exes, huh? Fun.”

“Something like that.” I was already lighting another from the pack I’d bought on the way over, because one wasn’t enough anymore. The smoke curled up, wrapping around both of us.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And Reyes was right—I was chasing him anyway.

Luca stepped closer again, pressing the cigarette to my lips. His voice was softer now, almost tired. “Tomorrow. The box. You in?”

I took the drag, held his gaze. “Yeah. I’m in.”

Stupid. So fucking stupid.

But as he walked away into the rain, lighter still in his pocket, I couldn’t make myself care. The smoke from my cigarette mixed with the downpour, and all I could think was how much worse this was going to get.

And how I was going to let it.

The motel was called the Starlite, which was a lie on every level. It squatted on the edge of the industrial district like a hangover that refused to die, neon sign flickering one letter at a time so it read “S A R L I T E.” Rain had been falling for three straight days now, turning the parking lot into a shallow lake of oil and regret. I’d spent the day chasing scraps. Two bartenders, one drag queen who owed me a favor, and a nervous numbers runner who swore Luca had been crashing here under the name “Smith.” Creative. I had the room number. I also had a headache and the taste of too many cigarettes in the back of my throat.

Room 17. The door was thin enough that I could hear the television inside murmuring some old Western. I didn’t knock soft. Two sharp raps, then I stepped back so he couldn’t see me through the peephole right away.

The door opened six inches, chain still on. Luca’s face appeared, hair messy, shirt unbuttoned to the sternum. His eyes widened a fraction when he saw me, then narrowed.

“You really don’t know when to quit.”

“Open the door, Luca.”

“Or what? You’ll shoot the lock like some dime-store cowboy?”

I showed him the bottle of cheap bourbon I’d brought like a peace offering. “Or I’ll drink this alone and leave you to whatever’s coming.”

He considered me for a long second. The cigarette smoke drifting out past his shoulder told me he’d been chain-smoking for hours. Finally the chain slid free and the door opened.

The room was what you’d expect: sagging double bed, water-stained ceiling, a nightstand with an overflowing ashtray. A half-eaten sandwich sat next to a cheap radio playing low static. Luca backed up until his legs hit the bed and sat down, watching me like I was a stray dog that might bite.

I closed the door, locked it, and set the bourbon on the dresser. “You left me with Reyes in that alley. Nice.”

“You handled it.” He reached for the pack on the nightstand, shook one out. His hands were shaking worse than yesterday. “He always that charming?”

“Worse, usually.” I took the lighter from my pocket—the one he hadn’t managed to steal yet—and flicked it for him. He leaned in, cupping my hand even though there was no wind. The flame lit up the hollow of his throat, the faint bruise I’d left there the night before. When he pulled back, smoke curled between us like a third person in the room.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas, and I was standing in a motel room with both.

“Talk,” I said.

Luca took a long drag, held it until his eyes watered, then let it out slow. “Ledger’s real. Pictures, names, dates. Moretti’s been running boys through the clubs for years. Blackmail, quiet disposals when they got too loud. I wasn’t supposed to see it. I just… got mad.”

“Mad enough to steal from a man who keeps a guy like Reyes on payroll.”

“Yeah, well.” He gave a bitter little laugh. “I’m not known for my impulse control.”

I crossed the small space and took the cigarette from his fingers. Took a drag myself. It tasted like him. Everything did now. “You used me as bait last night. Don’t lie. You let me find you so Reyes would see us together. Make it look like I’m the one stirring the pot.”

Luca didn’t deny it. He just watched me with those dark eyes, mouth soft around the lie he wasn’t telling. Then he reached up, took the cigarette back, and stubbed it out in the overflowing ashtray. The motion brought him close enough that I could see the faint tremor in his lower lip.

“I changed my mind,” he said quietly.

“About what?”

“About using you.”

The silence stretched. Outside, a truck rumbled past, splashing water against the window. Inside, the radio crackled with some forgotten love song. I should have walked out. Should have taken the information and left him to the wolves. Instead I stepped between his knees where he sat on the bed.

“This is stupid,” I told him.

“Probably.” His hands came up, sliding under my coat, fingers cold from the rain. “You gonna stop?”

“No.”

The kiss started where the alley one left off—angry, messy, too much teeth. He tasted like smoke and bourbon he must have drunk before I got there. I pushed him back onto the bed and he went willingly, legs wrapping around my hips like he’d been waiting for this exact disaster. The mattress groaned under us. The springs were shot.

Clothes came off in clumsy jerks. His leather jacket hit the floor. My shirt lost two buttons. When I got his pants open and took him in my hand he made a sound that was half laugh, half moan, like even in this he couldn’t be serious. I bit the side of his neck to shut him up and he arched so hard the headboard slammed the wall.

“Fuck, Jack—”

“Shut up.”

I wasn’t gentle. Neither was he. There was too much at stake and too little trust between us for gentle. It was all sweat and smoke and the stupid hungry way we kept chasing each other’s mouths. At one point he flipped us, straddling me, slim hips rolling with a rhythm that felt like punishment and prayer at the same time. His fingers dug bruises into my shoulders. Mine left marks on his thighs. The cigarette pack got knocked to the floor and scattered like tiny white bones.

When it was over we lay tangled in the cheap sheets that smelled like bleach and other people’s regret. Luca reached over me for the pack, lit two cigarettes at once with my lighter, and passed one down. We smoked in silence for a while, the smoke drifting up to join the water stains on the ceiling.

He spoke first. “I meant what I said. I wasn’t going to use you. Not after last night.”

“Bullshit.”

“Maybe.” He turned his head on the pillow. His hair was sticking up in every direction and there was a fresh hickey blooming under his jaw. He looked nineteen and forty at the same time. “The ledger’s in a safety deposit box at the old Merchants Bank. Key’s taped under the sink in the bathroom here. I was going to run with it tomorrow. Sell it to the highest bidder and get the hell out of this city.”

I took a drag, watched the smoke curl from my own mouth. It looked exactly like the smoke curling from his. “Why tell me now?”

“Because you’re still here.” His voice cracked just a little on the last word. He covered it with another drag. “Most guys would’ve taken the hint after Reyes showed up. You didn’t. Makes a guy think stupid things.”

I wanted to laugh. Wanted to tell him I was the one thinking stupid things—like how his shoulder fit under mine, how the way he stole lighters felt almost tender now. Instead I stubbed the cigarette out on the nightstand, right on top of the mess in the ashtray, and rolled toward him.

We didn’t talk after that. Just lay there while the rain beat the roof and the neon sign outside buzzed like dying insects. His breathing evened out first, but I didn’t trust it. I waited until his hand went slack on my chest, then slipped out of bed.

The key was exactly where he said—taped under the sink with two pieces of electrical tape. Small brass thing that felt heavier than it should. I pocketed it, pulled my clothes on, and stood over the bed for a long minute.

Luca looked younger asleep. Less dangerous. The cigarette burn on his forearm was visible now, an old scar shaped like a crude cross. I wondered who put it there. Wondered how many other marks he carried that I hadn’t seen yet.

I wrote a note on the back of a matchbook from the Blue Note. Three words: *We’ll talk tomorrow.* Then I left the half-empty bourbon on the nightstand like an apology.

Outside, the rain had eased to a drizzle. I lit a cigarette in the doorway of the Starlite Motel and watched the smoke drift across the parking lot. It twisted in the neon, wrapped around nothing, disappeared.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And I’d just fucked the biggest one yet.

I got in the car, started the engine, and drove away before I could change my mind and crawl back into that bed. In the rearview mirror the S A R L I T E sign blinked once, like it was laughing at me.

By the time I reached my apartment the note in my pocket felt like it was burning a hole. I poured three fingers of the good stuff I kept for emergencies, sat at the kitchen table, and stared at the key I’d taken.

The phone rang at four in the morning. I knew who it was before I picked up.

Reyes didn’t bother with hello. “You found him.”

“Yeah.”

“You sleep with him?”

“That’s not your business anymore, Frank.”

He laughed, low and ugly. “Everything’s my business when Moretti’s breathing down my neck. The ledger has my face in it, Jack. You hand that over to anyone but me and I’ll make sure both of you end up in the river. Understand?”

I understood. I understood too well.

I hung up without answering, lit another cigarette, and watched the smoke rise toward the cracked ceiling of my kitchen. It curled the same way it had around Luca’s throat in the bar. The same way it had in that shitty motel room while he slept.

Tomorrow I’d have to decide whose bad idea I was going to follow.

For now I just smoked, and tried not to think about how warm his skin had felt against mine, or how the note I left him was already starting to feel like a lie.

The cigarette burned down to the filter. I lit another off the stub.

Bad ideas, all the way down.
step_outputs.9:
The rain had finally stopped by morning, but the city still smelled wet and guilty. I spent the day doing exactly what I shouldn’t: drinking black coffee that tasted like engine grease, pacing my office until the floorboards creaked in protest, and thinking about Luca Vale in ways that had nothing to do with the ledger or the job.

I kept seeing him in that motel bed, smoke curling from his lips while his hands shook just enough to give him away. The way he’d said *I changed my mind about using you* like it cost him something. The key in my pocket felt heavier every hour. I turned it over and over until the brass warmed to body temperature, like it might confess something.

By noon I was on my third drink of the day, which broke every rule I pretended to have. I told myself it was medicinal. The truth was simpler: I was already hooked. He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas, and I was mainlining the habit.

I drank in the apartment instead of the office. The place was a railroad flat above a dry cleaner, two rooms that smelled permanently of starch and regret. I sat at the scarred kitchen table with the half-empty bourbon from the night before and watched the matchbooks I’d collected over the years. Blue Note. Sinkhole. Starlite Motel. Each one a tombstone for better judgment.

Reyes called twice. I let the phone ring into the void both times. His voice on the machine was calm, almost friendly, which meant he was furious. “Jack, don’t be stupid. Moretti’s crew is already asking questions. Bring the kid in. We can work something out.” Click. The second message was shorter. “You always were a sucker for a pretty liar. Call me before this gets messy.”

I poured another drink instead.

The afternoon slid into evening without my permission. I thought about the ledger, about the safety deposit box, about how many names in that book could end careers or lives. My own included, probably. But mostly I thought about the way Luca had looked sleeping, younger and almost soft, the burn scar on his arm catching the neon from the window.

By two in the morning I was drunk enough to admit I wasn’t going to walk away. I was still drunk enough not to care.

The knock on my door came like an answer to a question I hadn’t asked out loud.

I opened it with the .38 in my hand, because old habits. Luca stood in the hallway dripping wet even though the rain had stopped hours ago. He must have walked the whole way. His hair was plastered to his forehead, leather jacket dark with water, eyes big and tired and a little wild.

“You left me the key,” he said. No hello. No accusation. Just that flat, exhausted statement like it explained everything.

I lowered the gun. “Yeah.”

He stepped inside without being invited. The door clicked shut behind him and suddenly the apartment felt too small for both of us and all the smoke we carried. He smelled like rain and the same cheap cologne and the faint metallic tang of fear.

“I woke up and the key was gone,” he continued, shrugging out of the wet jacket. It hit the floor with a sad slap. “And there was this pathetic little note on a matchbook. *We’ll talk tomorrow.*” He laughed once, short and ugly. “You sounded like a fucking Hallmark card, Jack.”

I set the gun on the table next to the bourbon. “You came anyway.”

“Yeah. I did.” He looked around the kitchen like he was cataloging escape routes. His gaze landed on the empty glass, the overflowing ashtray, the half dozen matchbooks fanned out like evidence. “You’ve been thinking about me.”

It wasn’t a question.

I didn’t answer. Instead I crossed the room, caught him by the front of his damp shirt, and kissed him like I’d been waiting sixteen hours to do it. He made a surprised sound that turned into something hungrier. His hands came up, one fisting in my hair, the other sliding under my shirt like he needed skin immediately. We tasted like bourbon and rain and the particular bitterness of two men who knew better.

The kiss broke long enough for him to steal the cigarette from behind my ear. He lit it with my lighter—still in his possession from the alley, the thief—and took a drag before offering it back. We passed it back and forth while we stumbled toward the bedroom, shedding clothes like bad decisions.

The sex was slower this time but not gentler. There was too much history already, even after three days. He rode me with deliberate rolls of his hips, watching my face the whole time like he was memorizing how to ruin me. I kept one hand on his throat, not squeezing, just feeling the flutter of his pulse and the way the smoke from the shared cigarette kept drifting across his collarbones. Every time he leaned down to kiss me the cigarette ash tumbled onto my chest and he’d smear it with his thumb like marking territory.

Afterward we lay tangled in my shitty sheets that didn’t smell like bleach and strangers. The cigarette had burned down to nothing. Luca reached for the pack on the nightstand, lit two more. Passed one over without looking.

We smoked in the dark for a long time.

“You really were going to run with it,” I said finally.

“Yeah.” His voice was quiet in the dark. “Still might. The box is at Merchants on Fourth. Key works for box 217. There’s twenty grand in cash and the ledger. Enough to disappear.”

“Why tell me?”

He turned his head on the pillow. In the faint light from the street his eyes looked almost soft. Almost. “Because every time I try to leave you behind I end up on your doorstep instead. That’s new for me.”

I wanted to believe him. That was the problem.

The silence stretched. I could hear the dripping from the fire escape, the distant wail of a siren, the wet sound of him pulling on the cigarette. He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas, and I was letting him turn my apartment into an ashtray for both of us.

A new sound cut through the quiet—my front door creaking open.

I was up with the gun before my brain caught up. Luca rolled off the bed in one smooth motion, naked and reaching for the knife he apparently kept in his boot even when he took everything else off. We moved like we’d done this before.

Reyes stepped into the bedroom doorway like he owned it. Coat still on, badge visible, gun already out but pointed at the floor. His eyes took in the scene: the tangled sheets, the two naked men, the smoke still hanging in the air like evidence.

“Well,” he said, voice flat. “This is charming.”

“Frank.” My voice came out rough. “You don’t have a key.”

“I have lots of things.” His gaze slid to Luca, who hadn’t bothered covering up. Luca just stood there, knife loose in his hand, cigarette still burning between two fingers of the other. The ash was getting long again. “Cute. You two playing house now?”

Luca smiled, the mean one. “Jealous, Detective? He fucks better when he’s angry.”

Reyes’s jaw tightened. I stepped between them before this turned into something I couldn’t take back.

“What do you want, Frank?”

“The ledger. Moretti’s getting impatient. He’s got people watching the Velvet Room. Two of Teddy’s boys got worked over tonight. Next it’ll be worse.” His eyes flicked to me again. Something almost like hurt lived in them for a second. “I told you to walk away, Jack. You never listen.”

Luca exhaled smoke toward the ceiling. “Maybe he likes bad ideas more than he likes you.”

“Luca,” I warned.

Reyes laughed once, short and bitter. “He’s not wrong. You always picked the pretty ones who’d get you killed. First me, now him.” He lowered his gun completely. “Bring me the ledger tomorrow. Both of you. Merchants Bank, noon. We’ll do the exchange quiet. Moretti gets his book, you two get to live. Otherwise I can’t protect you.”

He looked at the burn scar on Luca’s arm, then at the matching bruises on my neck. His mouth twisted.

“Nice scars,” he said to Luca. “You collect them like matchbooks.”

Then he was gone, footsteps heavy on the hallway floor. The front door clicked shut like a period at the end of a bad sentence.

I stood there naked with a gun in my hand and a man I barely knew breathing behind me. Luca stepped close, pressed his chest to my back, and reached around to take the cigarette from my fingers. He took a drag, then offered it back.

“Tomorrow,” he said against my shoulder.

“Yeah.”

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And now we were both in it up to our necks, with Reyes holding the rope.

I took the cigarette, felt the burn in my lungs, and wondered how many more drags I had left before the whole thing went up in flames.

The smoke rose between us in the dark, curling like a question neither of us wanted to answer.
step_outputs.10:
The apartment smelled like smoke, sweat, and yesterday’s bad decisions. We didn’t leave for three days.

Luca stayed. I let him. That was the first stupid thing.

We kept the curtains drawn and the lights low. The only illumination came from the neon across the street bleeding pink and green through the gaps in the blinds. It painted stripes across his bare back while he slept, or didn’t sleep, or pretended to. The radio stayed on low, some late-night station playing old standards that made everything feel like a movie nobody asked to be in.

Most of the time we didn’t talk about the ledger.

We talked about nothing instead. He stole my last clean shirt and wore it like a dress, sleeves rolled up past his elbows. The burn scar on his forearm caught the neon every time he reached for a cigarette. I never asked who gave it to him. He never offered.

On the second night—or maybe the third, time got slippery—he sat on the kitchen counter in nothing but that shirt and his socks, legs swinging like a kid. I stood between his knees drinking warm bourbon straight from the bottle because I couldn’t be bothered with a glass anymore.

“You ever think about quitting this city?” he asked.

“Every morning I wake up here.”

He took the bottle from me, drank, handed it back. His fingers brushed mine and stayed there longer than necessary. “I could sell the ledger in Chicago. Guy I know runs a club. Pays cash, no questions. We could be gone before Moretti even wakes up.”

We. The word landed between us like a lit match on dry carpet.

I took a swig, felt it burn all the way down. “There’s no we, Luca. There’s you with your stolen book and me with my shitty office and the fact that Reyes still has my spare key.”

He laughed softly, the mean one that didn’t reach his eyes. “You keep saying that. Yet here I am wearing your shirt and you’re letting me.” His hand slid up my chest, fingers splayed over my heart like he was checking if it still worked. “You gonna throw me out now?”

I didn’t answer. Instead I kissed him so hard the bottle tipped over and spilled across the counter. Neither of us reached to stop it. The bourbon ran into the sink like it was trying to escape.

The sex that followed wasn’t like the motel or the first night in the alley. It wasn’t even like the night Reyes walked in on us. This was slower, meaner, more honest. He rode me on the kitchen floor with the spilled bourbon sticky under my back and his nails digging crescents into my shoulders. Every time I tried to touch him gently he slapped my hands away.

“Don’t,” he hissed against my mouth. “Don’t you dare get soft on me, Jack.”

So I didn’t. I fucked him like I hated him. Like I hated myself for needing this. He came with my name in his throat and his teeth in my collarbone, hard enough to bruise. Afterward we lay there on the dirty linoleum, breathing like we’d run ten blocks from the law. The cigarette he lit tasted like bourbon and blood where I’d bitten his lip.

He passed it to me without a word. We shared it until it burned our fingers.

That was the night he finally talked.

We’d moved to the bed by then. The sheets smelled like both of us now. He lay on his stomach, chin on his folded arms, watching me smoke. The neon painted green across the sharp line of his jaw.

“I wasn’t lying about why I took it,” he said quietly. “Moretti’s guys came into the Velvet Room looking for fresh meat. I was singing that night. They picked a kid named Mikey. Nineteen. Pretty. Stupid. I told them to fuck off. Next morning Mikey showed up with a broken jaw and that ledger in his pocket. Moretti’s little insurance policy. Names, photos, dates. Including your ex.”

I didn’t look at him. Just watched the smoke rise and curl above us like it was writing the rest of the story.

Luca kept going. “I was supposed to deliver the kid back to the club the next night. Instead I took the ledger and ran. Figured I could sell it, get enough money to disappear, maybe send some cash to Mikey’s sister. Then Teddy hired you.” He gave a small, tired laugh. “Didn’t expect you to be so… persistent.”

I took a long drag. The smoke burned. “You planned to use me as a shield. Still do.”

“Yeah.” No apology in his voice. “At first. Then you kissed me in the rain and looked at me like I was something worth saving. That fucked everything up.”

I turned my head. His eyes were dark, unreadable. The cigarette between my fingers was almost gone. “I’m not saving anybody, Luca. Least of all you.”

“Liar.” He reached over, took the cigarette, took the last drag, and stubbed it out on the windowsill. The burn mark joined three others already there. My windowsill was starting to look like his personal ashtray. “You could’ve turned me over to Reyes three times now. You haven’t. That key’s been in your pocket for days and you still haven’t opened that box without me.”

He was right. That was the worst part.

I rolled on top of him before he could say anything else. Pinned his wrists above his head with one hand. He let me. His legs opened without being asked. When I pushed back inside him he gasped, head tipping back, throat exposed. I bit the scar under his jaw and he moaned like it hurt and felt perfect at the same time.

We fucked like the argument wasn’t over. Like the fight itself was foreplay. He cursed me in two languages and laughed breathlessly when I cursed back. When we finally came it was almost angry, like we were punishing each other for caring even a little.

After, he curled against my side without asking permission. His head on my chest, one leg thrown over mine. The position felt too intimate for what we were. I lit another cigarette one-handed and smoked it while his breathing evened out.

The smoke curled up toward the ceiling, lazy and familiar. It wrapped around the light fixture like it belonged there. I watched it and thought about how every drag was another bad decision I wasn’t quitting.

Luca’s voice came soft in the dark, half-asleep. “I was going to leave you the key and disappear. That night at the motel. I wrote a note and everything. Then I saw you standing there with your sad cop eyes and I couldn’t do it.”

I didn’t answer. Just kept smoking.

He shifted, pressed his lips to the scar on my ribs from a knife fight eight years ago. “You’re terrible for me, Jack Moss.”

“Feeling’s mutual.”

He hummed like that pleased him. A few minutes later his breathing changed into real sleep. I stayed awake, cigarette burning down to the filter, watching the smoke make lazy patterns in the neon glow.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And I was starting to think the ideas weren’t the only thing I was addicted to.

The phone rang at dawn. I let it ring. Reyes again, probably. Or Teddy wondering where his ledger was. I didn’t care. I just lay there with Luca’s warm weight against me and the taste of shared cigarettes in my mouth.

Tomorrow we’d go to the bank. Tomorrow we’d decide whether to sell the ledger, burn it, or hand it to the highest bidder. Tomorrow the real world would come crashing back in with guns and consequences.

For now there was only the smoke, the neon, and the stupid, inevitable pull of the man sleeping on my chest like he belonged there.

I lit another cigarette off the stub of the last one.

Bad idea.

I took a drag anyway.
step_outputs.11:
The Merchants Bank building looked like it had been dying since 1929. Granite steps worn smooth by generations of liars and thieves, brass doors that still gleamed with false respectability. Luca and I stood across the street under a sagging awning, sharing the last cigarette from my pack while the morning drizzle turned the sidewalk into a mirror of bad reflections.

He looked like shit and somehow still beautiful. Two days of hiding in my apartment had left shadows under his eyes and a nervous twitch in his left hand. The burn scar on his forearm showed every time he pushed up the sleeve of my stolen shirt. I wore the same coat I’d had on the night we met. It still smelled like both of us.

“Box 217,” he muttered, passing me the cigarette. “Third row, bottom left. Key should work. Cash in a manila envelope. Ledger in a plain black notebook. Nothing fancy.”

“Nothing fancy,” I repeated. The smoke tasted sour. My head still hurt from the bourbon and the sex and the fact that I hadn’t slept more than three hours in three days. “You sure nobody’s watching this place?”

Luca gave me that mean little smile. “Positive? No. Hopeful? Yeah.”

We crossed the street. My hand stayed near the .38 under my coat. His stayed in his pocket, probably wrapped around the cheap switchblade he thought I didn’t know about. The bank lobby was almost empty. One old woman at the teller window, a bored security guard reading a racing form, and a clerk who looked like he’d rather be anywhere else.

Luca handled the paperwork with the ease of someone who’d done this dance before. Fake ID. Signature that didn’t match the name. The clerk barely glanced at either of us. We were escorted down to the vault by a skinny kid in a cheap suit who kept clearing his throat like he had something stuck in it.

The safety deposit boxes gleamed under fluorescent lights. Box 217 looked exactly like the others. Luca slid the key in. It turned with a soft click that felt too loud.

Inside: the manila envelope thick with cash, the black notebook, and a small revolver I hadn’t expected. Luca’s eyes flicked to it, then to me. He slipped the gun into his jacket without a word.

We were halfway back up the stairs when the first shot came.

It wasn’t dramatic. No slow-motion chase music. Just the flat crack of a .45 from the lobby above us and the clerk’s surprised grunt as he went down. The skinny kid in the cheap suit screamed once and ran. Smart.

Luca shoved me against the wall. “Back door. There’s an alley—”

Another shot. This one splintered the wooden banister six inches from my head. I grabbed his arm and dragged him down the remaining stairs, through the employees-only door, and out into the service corridor that smelled like bleach and panic.

We ran.

The alley behind the bank was narrow and slick with rain. Two men were already waiting—one built like a refrigerator, the other skinny and mean with a face like a rat. Moretti’s crew. They must have followed us from my apartment. Or Reyes had given us up. Either option felt equally likely.

The big one raised his gun. I put two rounds in his chest before he could squeeze the trigger. The sound bounced off the brick walls like thunder. The skinny one got off a wild shot that clipped Luca’s left arm. I saw the blood bloom before I heard him swear.

“Fuck—”

I grabbed him, shoved him behind a dumpster, and returned fire. The skinny guy went down screaming, clutching his knee. Not dead, but he wasn’t chasing anybody soon.

Luca was breathing hard, blood running down his fingers onto the wet pavement. The wound looked like a graze, but it was bleeding enough to scare me more than it should have. I tore a strip off the bottom of my shirt and tied it tight around his bicep. My hands were shaking.

“You good?” I asked.

He laughed, the sound thin and pained. “Define good.”

Another shot from the mouth of the alley. This one came from a different direction. I risked a look and saw Reyes standing there in his good coat, gun steady, face unreadable. Two more of Moretti’s men flanked him like the loyal dogs they were.

“Jack!” Reyes called out. His voice echoed off the bricks. “Last chance. Toss the ledger over and I’ll let you walk. The kid too. Mostly.”

Luca pressed his forehead against my shoulder for a second. Just one second. Then he straightened, took the revolver from his jacket with his good hand, and checked the cylinder like a man who’d done it a thousand times.

“He’s lying,” Luca whispered. “He’ll kill us both the second he has it.”

“I know.”

I looked at him then. Really looked. The blood on his arm, the ash from an earlier cigarette still smudged on his jaw, the way his mouth kept trying to smile even though his eyes were terrified. He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas, and I was about to die in an alley with him.

The realization didn’t feel as bad as it should have.

We moved at the same time.

I came out from behind the dumpster firing. One of Moretti’s men dropped. Reyes returned fire, cool and professional, the way he’d taught me years ago. A bullet tugged at my coat sleeve. Another shattered the window above my head, showering me with glass.

Luca was right beside me, shooting left-handed and cursing beautifully in Italian. He caught the second gunman in the throat. The man went down gurgling.

Then it was just Reyes.

He stood at the end of the alley, gun lowered but not put away. Blood on his cheek from flying glass. His eyes met mine across twenty feet of wet pavement and spent casings.

“You always were terrible at following orders, Moss.”

“Yeah, well. You always were a shitty lay.”

Reyes smiled like that actually hurt him. Then he raised the gun again.

Luca moved faster than I expected. He stepped in front of me just as Reyes fired. The bullet took him high in the shoulder, spinning him around like a drunk dancer. He hit the ground hard, the black ledger sliding from his jacket and landing in a puddle.

I put three rounds into Reyes before he could fire again. Two in the chest, one in the head. He dropped without a sound, eyes still open, looking surprised that it had finally come to this.

The alley went quiet except for the rain and Luca’s ragged breathing.

I knelt beside him. The new wound was worse than the graze. Blood soaked the front of my stolen shirt. His face had gone gray. The revolver had fallen from his fingers but he was still trying to reach for the ledger like it mattered.

“Leave it,” I said. My voice cracked.

“Gotta… burn it…”

“Shut up.”

I pressed my hands over the wound. Blood welled between my fingers, warm and sticky. His eyes fluttered open, found mine. That terrible, beautiful mouth tried for a smile.

“Told you I changed my mind about using you,” he whispered. “Looks like I took a bullet for you instead. Romantic, huh?”

“Shut up, Luca.”

He coughed. Blood on his lip. I wiped it away with my thumb, probably getting more on him than off. The rain was mixing with the blood on the pavement, turning everything pink.

The sound of sirens rose in the distance. Someone must have called it in. We had minutes at most.

I gathered him up, ledger be damned, and half-carried, half-dragged him out of the alley toward the street. The black notebook lay in the puddle behind us, pages starting to dissolve in the rain. Good. Let it rot.

Luca’s head lolled against my shoulder. His breathing was too shallow.

“Don’t you fucking die on me,” I told him. “Not after all this stupid smoke and all these bad ideas.”

His laugh was barely a sound. “Too late… already did the bad idea part…”

I kept moving. One foot in front of the other. Blood on my hands. Smoke still clinging to both our clothes from the cigarette we’d shared an hour ago. Sirens getting closer.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And I was carrying him through the rain wondering how the hell I was going to live without either one.
step_outputs.12:
The warehouse smelled like dead fish and rust. We’d made it six blocks before Luca’s legs gave out completely. I half-dragged him through three alleys and a broken fence, leaving a trail of blood that a blind man could follow. The ledger was gone, dissolved in that alley puddle, but Moretti’s remaining crew didn’t know that yet. Neither did the cops.

I kicked open a side door on Pier 17’s abandoned canning warehouse. Inside was all shadows and dripping pipes. Moonlight cut through the high broken windows in dirty silver slices. I lowered Luca onto a stack of rotting pallets, his back against a concrete pillar. Blood had soaked through both wounds now. The shoulder was worse. His face looked like old paper.

“Stay with me,” I said.

He tried for that mean little smile. It came out as a grimace. “Where would I go? Got a hot date with a bullet.”

I tore more of my shirt, made a fresh pad, pressed it hard against the shoulder. He hissed but didn’t pull away. His good hand came up and gripped my wrist, not pushing me off, just holding on. His fingers were cold.

The sirens had faded, but that didn’t mean we were safe. Reyes was dead in that alley. That would bring heat—cop heat, mob heat, everybody who owed him favors or feared him. I had maybe twenty minutes before someone figured out where the blood trail led.

Luca coughed. A wet sound. “You killed him. Your ex. For me.”

“Yeah.”

“Feel anything?”

I looked at him. Really looked. The neon was gone. Only moonlight now, carving his cheekbones sharp, turning the sweat on his skin to silver. Ash from earlier cigarettes still dusted his collar. He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas, even bleeding out in a fish warehouse.

“Feels like I should feel more,” I said. “But mostly I just want another cigarette and for you to stop bleeding on my last clean shirt.”

He laughed. It turned into a cough that brought up blood. I wiped it from his mouth with my thumb. The gesture felt too tender for the both of us. He noticed.

“Getting soft, Jack Moss.”

“Shut up.”

We sat in the quiet for a minute. Pipes dripped. Somewhere outside a tugboat horn sounded low and mournful. I pulled the last two cigarettes from my crumpled pack, lit them both off one match, and put one between his lips. His hand shook too badly to hold it steady, so I kept it there for him, letting him drag while I held the filter.

“Reyes used to say I had shit taste in men,” I told him. “Guess he was right.”

Luca took a shallow pull. Smoke curled up between us, thin and gray in the moonlight. “I was gonna leave you the key that night at the motel. Had the note written and everything. Then you stood there looking at me like I was worth the trouble. Stupid. Both of us.”

“Yeah.”

His head tipped back against the pillar. Eyes half-lidded. “I steal things, Jack. Lighters. Money. People’s last cigarette. Never could keep anything good. Always figured I’d die young and messy. Just didn’t think I’d mind so much anymore.”

The words landed heavy. I took my own drag, felt the burn, watched the smoke twist around his throat like it always did. Like it belonged there.

“Stop talking like you’re checking out,” I said. “You’re not allowed to die in a fucking warehouse. That’s too cliché even for us.”

He smiled around the cigarette. Blood on his teeth. “Cliché’s all we got left.”

Footsteps outside. Heavy. Multiple. I pulled the .38, checked the cylinder. Three rounds left. Not enough. Luca saw it and reached for his switchblade with his good hand. The blade flicked out with a soft snick. Pathetic arsenal against what was coming.

The side door banged open. Three men this time. Moretti’s remaining muscle and one I recognized from the Velvet Room—a rat-faced driver who used to run bets for Teddy. They fanned out, guns up. The leader, a thick-necked guy with a scar across his nose, spotted us against the pillar.

“Vale. Moss. Should’ve stayed hidden.”

Luca coughed another laugh. “Hide better next time. Write that down.”

I stood up slowly, keeping myself between them and Luca. The .38 felt light in my hand. “Ledger’s gone. Dissolved in the rain. No copies. It’s over.”

Scar-nose didn’t look convinced. “Boss wants proof. Or bodies. We got orders either way.”

The rat-faced one smiled like Christmas came early. “Reyes is dead. You did us a favor there. But you also made a mess. Moretti don’t like messes.”

They started closing in. I raised the gun. Luca tried to push himself up beside me but his legs wouldn’t hold. He stayed on his knees, switchblade ready, breathing like each breath cost him something.

First gunshot came from the left. I fired back, caught the rat-faced guy in the gut. He folded. Second man got a round off that whined past my ear and buried in the concrete. I put my last two bullets in Scar-nose—one in the chest, one in the throat. He dropped like a sack of wet concrete.

The third man—a skinny kid who looked about nineteen—panicked. He emptied his clip wild. One bullet caught me in the side, just above the hip. Burning pain, but not deep. I felt the blood start immediately. The kid turned to run. Luca threw the switchblade with his good arm. It sank into the kid’s back, low. He went down screaming.

Then it was quiet again except for the dripping pipes and three new bodies.

I staggered back to Luca. The pain in my side was a steady throb now. He looked worse. Face gray, lips blue at the edges. But his eyes were still open, still tracking me.

“You’re hit,” he said.

“So are you. Twice.”

“Fair’s fair.”

I knelt in front of him. The warehouse smelled like gunpowder and blood now, underneath the fish stink. I pressed my hand to his shoulder again. The bleeding had slowed some, but not enough. My own blood was soaking into my waistband.

We looked at each other for a long moment. No smoke between us this time. The cigarettes had burned out on the floor.

Luca reached up with bloody fingers and touched the side of my face. The gesture was surprisingly gentle. “I was never gonna sell it, you know. Not really. Just needed someone to… see me. Before it all went to shit.”

“I see you,” I said. My voice came out rough. “Been seeing you since that first bar. Cigarette smoke and bad ideas. Whole package.”

He smiled. Real this time. No meanness in it. “Yeah. You too, Jack. Sad eyes and all.”

The sirens were coming back. Closer now. Red and blue lights began to strobe through the high windows. We had minutes.

I gathered him up again. He weighed less than he should. We stumbled toward the far end of the warehouse where an old loading dock faced the river. No more running. Just this.

Behind us, the bodies lay in the moonlight. Reyes somewhere across town in his own puddle of blood. The ledger gone. The job finished the only way it could.

Luca’s head rested against my good shoulder. His breathing was shallow but steady.

“Bad idea,” he whispered.

“Worst one yet,” I agreed.

We reached the dock. The river stretched out black and endless. City lights glittered on the far side like stars that didn’t give a shit. I lowered us both to the concrete, backs against a rusted bollard. My side burned. His shoulder kept leaking. We were a matching set.

I found one last cigarette in my pocket, bent but not broken. Lit it with the last match. Held it to his lips first. He took a drag, coughed once, then nodded. I took the next one. We passed it back and forth while the sirens grew louder.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And I was still choosing it. Still choosing him.

The red and blue lights finally reached the warehouse. Doors slammed. Voices shouted commands. I kept my arm around Luca’s shoulders, his head against my neck, the cigarette burning down between our fingers.

No more running.

Just this last drag together in the dark, waiting to see what fresh hell the morning would bring.

The smoke curled up one final time, thin and gray and perfect, wrapping around both of us like it had from the very first night.

Bad ideas.

All the way down.
step_outputs.13:
The sirens died like they’d changed their minds.

We sat on the loading dock with our backs against the rusted bollard, the river sliding past black and indifferent below us. The cigarette had burned down to the filter. I dropped it and watched the ember hiss out in a puddle of someone’s blood—mine, Luca’s, didn’t matter anymore. The warehouse behind us had gone quiet again. No more footsteps. No more guns. Just the drip of pipes and the low groan of the city waking up somewhere beyond the pier.

Luca’s head was heavy on my good shoulder. His breathing had that wet, ragged edge that usually meant the end of the story, but he was still conscious. Still stealing my warmth like he stole everything else.

“Reyes is dead,” I said, because one of us had to say it out loud.

“Yeah.” His voice was thin. “You put three in him. I counted.”

I looked down at my hands. They were shaking. One of them was wrapped around the grip of the empty .38 like it still mattered. The other was pressed to the hole in my side. Blood had slowed to a seep. Luca’s shoulder had stopped leaking too, which was either good news or the worst kind.

Sirens again, but farther off this time. Different direction. Maybe they’d found Reyes first. Maybe they were still chasing ghosts. I didn’t much care.

Luca shifted, winced, and reached into his jacket with his good hand. He came out with a crumpled pack I didn’t recognize. Two cigarettes left. He shook one out, stuck it between his teeth, and looked at me expectantly.

I found the lighter—his now, or mine, who could tell anymore—and lit it for him. The flame showed his face: gray skin, dark eyes still too sharp, that mouth that had caused every problem I currently had. He took a drag, coughed once, then offered it back like a communion wafer.

We shared it in silence while the sky turned the color of dirty dishwater. Dawn. The city didn’t care that we’d just burned down half our lives. It never did.

“You burned the ledger,” he said after a while.

“In the alley. Rain finished the job.”

“Good.”

He sounded almost peaceful about it. The man who’d stolen the thing in the first place now sounded relieved it was gone. I took my turn with the cigarette, felt the smoke curl down into my lungs like an old friend who’d overstayed his welcome.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And I was still here with him.

“We should move,” I said.

“Can’t feel my legs.”

“Shit.”

I stubbed the cigarette out on the concrete. The second one stayed in the pack. We might need it later. I got my good arm under him and hauled us both up. He made a sound that wasn’t quite a scream but came close. We staggered along the dock like two drunks after last call, leaving dark wet footprints behind us.

My car was still parked three blocks away, if nobody had stolen it or turned it into a crime scene. We headed in that direction because there was nothing else to do. Every step sent fresh pain through my side. Luca was leaning heavier with every yard. His breath came in short, pissed-off gasps.

Halfway there he stopped, sagged against a chain-link fence, and laughed.

Actual laughter. Weak, but real.

“What?” I asked.

“We’re a fucking mess, Jack. Look at us. Two grown men leaking all over the street because we couldn’t keep our dicks and our morals in separate rooms.”

“Speak for yourself. My morals were never in the picture.”

He smiled at that. The split in his lip opened again. Blood mixed with the rainwater still drying on his face. “Liar. You could’ve handed me over night one. Instead you fucked me in a motel, let me bleed on your kitchen floor, and shot your ex for me. That’s not nothing.”

I didn’t have an answer that wasn’t embarrassing. So I kissed him instead. Right there against the fence with the sky turning gray and the city starting to notice us. He tasted like blood and the last cigarette and every stupid choice I’d made since I first saw him through that haze of smoke. His good hand fisted in my ruined coat. Mine cupped the back of his neck like I could hold him together by sheer stubbornness.

When we broke apart he was breathing harder.

“Bad idea,” he whispered against my mouth.

“Worst one yet.”

We kept walking.

The car was still there. Miracle of small mercies. I got him into the passenger seat, climbed behind the wheel, and drove with one hand pressed to my side. Blood kept seeping between my fingers and onto the upholstery. Luca’s head lolled against the window, eyes half-open, watching the city slide past.

We left the river behind. Drove north through streets that were just waking up. Delivery trucks. Early shift workers with coffee in paper cups. Nobody looked at us. We looked like any other pair of assholes who’d had a rough night.

After twenty minutes Luca spoke again. His voice was softer now.

“I don’t have anywhere to go.”

“Neither do I. Office is burned. Apartment’s probably being watched. Reyes had friends.”

He nodded like that was exactly what he expected. Then he reached over and put his hand on my thigh. Not sexual. Just there. Warm. Shaking a little.

“I was gonna run to Chicago,” he said. “Had a contact. But the thought of doing it alone felt… worse than getting shot.”

“Romantic.”

“Shut up.”

I did. For a while. The sun was fully up now, turning the streets the color of cigarette ash. I drove us out of the city proper, onto the old state highway that led toward nothing special. No plan. No destination. Just away.

Luca lit the last cigarette one-handed. He took a drag, then held it to my lips so I could take one without letting go of the wheel or my side. We passed it back and forth like we’d been doing it for years instead of days.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And I was driving toward more of both.

We crested a small rise. The city sprawled behind us in the rearview, gray and wet and already forgetting us. Ahead was just road and trees and the kind of future that didn’t come with guarantees.

Luca broke the silence again.

“You know this doesn’t fix anything. I’m still a thief. You’re still a burned-out ex-cop who shoots people. We’re both probably wanted for something by now.”

“Yep.”

“I’ll probably steal your lighter again tomorrow.”

“Probably.”

He turned his head to look at me. The morning light showed every flaw—the split lip, the bruises, the exhaustion. He looked perfect.

“So what now?” he asked.

I took the cigarette from him, took the last drag, and flicked it out the window. The smoke trailed behind us for a second before the wind tore it apart.

“Now we find a motel that doesn’t ask questions. We get some sleep. We wake up tomorrow and figure out the next bad idea. Maybe we keep driving. Maybe we don’t. But we do it together until one of us gets bored or dead.”

Luca laughed again, softer this time. It didn’t sound like it hurt as much.

“Sounds like a plan.”

“It’s not.”

“Good.”

He leaned his head against my shoulder as best he could with the console in the way. His hand stayed on my thigh. The bleeding had mostly stopped. We’d need stitches, antibiotics, new names. None of that seemed urgent right now.

The road unspooled ahead of us, empty and open. I kept one hand on the wheel and the other on the wound in my side like both were equally important.

In the rearview mirror the city shrank to a smear of smoke and neon and bad memories. Reyes was back there somewhere, eyes open to the rain. The ledger was pulp. Teddy would be looking for us. Moretti’s crew would regroup.

None of it mattered as much as the man bleeding quietly in my passenger seat.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

And I was apparently into that.

I reached over, found his hand, and laced our fingers together. Sticky with blood. Neither of us let go.

The sun climbed higher. The road kept going.

We drove toward whatever came next, already lighting up the next stupid cigarette in our minds.

Bad ideas.

All the way down the highway.

[Analysis]

This chapter is a confident, well-executed piece of neo-noir writing that largely delivers on its plan and the broader story's intentions. Let me break it down critically.

STRENGTHS:

The voice is the chapter's greatest asset. Jack's first-person narration is genuinely lived-in—dry, self-mocking, and observant without tipping into parody. Lines like "my eyes had apparently decided to make him their full-time job" and "I kissed him instead. Harder than last night. Like punishment." feel earned rather than performed. The voice stays consistent throughout: crude when it needs to be, precise when it matters, never trying too hard.

The dialogue is notably strong. The exchange between Jack and Luca crackles with genuine tension—the banter feels like two people actually circling each other rather than two characters delivering exposition. "You gonna arrest me or kiss me" doesn't appear verbatim, but the spirit of Luca's character voice is well-maintained. The lighter theft as a character beat is excellent—it's shown, not told, and it perfectly illustrates Luca's need for small control. Reyes's entrance and his dialogue ("You always did have shit taste") lands with appropriate menace and echoes the character profile's voice examples naturally.

The sensory texture is handled well without becoming purple. Smoke, rain, cheap cologne, the damp cigarette filter—these accumulate without becoming a checklist. The detail of Luca pressing his own cigarette between Jack's lips is a genuinely good moment: intimate, transgressive, and character-revealing simultaneously.

The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the after-hours club, the lighter theft, the alley kiss, Reyes's warning, and Luca's vanishing act (modified here to a departure rather than a full disappearance, which actually works better dramatically). The safety deposit box setup for Chapter 6 is planted naturally.

WEAKNESSES:

The chapter occasionally reaches for a poetic note that doesn't quite land. "Glasses clinking like breaking promises" is the most egregious example—it's exactly the kind of noir-ish simile that sounds good for half a second before you realize it's hollow. "Taillights bleeding red into the rain" is a cliché that the chapter's otherwise grounded voice doesn't need. These are minor but worth noting.

The Reyes entrance, while well-executed, is slightly too convenient—he appears at exactly the right moment with exactly the right information. The chapter plan called for this, so it's not a deviation, but it's the most mechanically "plot-functional" moment in an otherwise organically flowing chapter.

Luca's characterization is excellent but occasionally tips toward archetype rather than individual. The "wicked mouth" and "magnetic" qualities are present but the chapter could do slightly more to show the exhaustion underneath his games that the character profile emphasizes. The moment where "something almost like regret" flickers under his smirk is good but brief.

The phrase "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas" appears twice in the chapter—once near the opening and once near the close. This is intentional and mostly works as a structural echo, but the second instance feels slightly mechanical, like the chapter is reminding itself of its own thesis.

The chapter is not amateurish. It's competent to genuinely good. The queerness is handled naturally—the underground club world, the fear of exposure implicit in Reyes's presence, the way these men exist in the margins—without lecturing. The moral grayness is maintained. Neither man is improved or redeemed.

Overall: a strong chapter that delivers on its promises with only minor lapses into noir cliché.
